SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with Trummy Young
by Patricia Willard
Tapes 1-3

Washington, D. C.
September 17 & 18, 1976

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

Interview with Trummy Young, September 17, 1976. Trummy, according to all of the authorities that I looked up they all agree that you were born the 12th of January, 1912 in Savannah, Georgia. Is that right?
Correct. That's correct.
And that your name is James Osborne Young.
That's right too, yeah.
And I see that you were raised in Washington, D. C. How long did you live in Savannah, Georgia?

Well, I was born in 1912, as you just brought up, and I lived there until 1926. And so, I got to see quite a bit of Savannah before I left, you know, because in those formative years I saw quite a few things down there. I was born in a section of Savannah called Yamacraw. It was an Indian section. And as you know, there was an Indian river that ran through there, the Ogeechee River.

And, well, in this particular section of Savannah there was a conglomeration of Negroes, Indians, and some Italians that I grew up with in this neighborhood. In later years, after about five or six years, when I was about nine, I imagine, we moved to a section of Savannah called Lovers Lane, and that was on another side, the east side. Of course, Yamacraw was on the west side.

And over there was where I met many of the old blues singers around there. Many of them didn't become famous but they worked in the turpentine fields around Savannah. Turpentine was a big thing that they had around there because ships would come in -- Savannah's a seaport -- and they would ship out this rosin and stuff that they would get from these trees.

But these guys were top blues singers, some of them around. They never got known. But then there are many bands that came through Savannah because it was right on that sea-board going from -- down to Florida. And the ministrel shows in the days I came up would come through there, shows like Dr. Rabbitfoot. These were where they had the old comedians, and these guys would sell medicine, the medicine shows. And they would make quite a bit of money from selling these -- this medicine. And there was no tax in those days. And they sold it.

But they would do a little show to attract people. They would put up a tent on a corner, and they didn't pay any rent for these corners. They'd just take a vacant lot and put these tents up. And they would attract quite a bit of attention. They all had bands, small orchestras with them, at least a drum, and a banjo, and perhaps some of them had a trombone player, maybe a trumpet player, and most had a clarinet player. One of the top clarinet players I ever met, Wilton Crawley, he

was a comedian, and he was also a clarinetist.

And he used to put a glass on his head, and he'd play the clarinet all between his legs, and do the splits and all. He was quite famous back in those days. And wherever he played on any of these medicine shows they were sure to have a big crowd.

And I watched quite a few fellows, and then I had an opportunity down there to watch a marching band but they played jazz from Charleston, South Carolina, which is only about 100 or so miles from Savannah. And this was the Jenkins Orphan Band. And before I left in 1926, why this band would come there. And he had some good musicians in there.

And we would follow them. Kids -- we would just follow them all down the streets, you know, because they reminded me a lot of that band that you see today from Grambling University because they did dance steps and they played jazz and they marched down the streets.
Was that the same band that Cat Anderson played in at one time? I know he was in some orphans --

Well, this was before Cat's time, you know, this was. But Jabbo Smith played in this orchestra, the trumpet player, and also there was a trombone player played in that orchestra named John Nick, N-i-c-k. And he was a fantastic trombone player. I never knew what happened to him
in later years, but he could play very good. And I would follow that band as a kid all down the street. I think I'm a little older than Cat, so this would have been a little --
A little bit older?
Yeah, before --
A lot.
-- Cat's time, yeah. Well, I'm a little older, yeah. I'll put it that way. But Cat might have played in one of those bands, but I didn't know him when he --
I wasn't sure about which -- the name of it, whether it was Jenkins or another one.
Well, Jenkins was from Charleston, South Carolina. I don't know where Cat was from originally.
Originally I can't remember either.
No.
The neighborhood that you lived in originally in Savannah, was that unusual in the South to have an integrated neighborhood at that time?

No, because actually at that time, except for maybe the Italians. But Indians, and Negroes, and even Chinese, they usually went to the same schools. There was a Chinese boy who lives in New York now that I went to school with, Tommy Ewing. And he has a sister, Olivia Ewing, and we all went to the same school, East Broad School in Savannah.

I never forgot that, you know.
But the Italians, they lived in that district, but they usually were on a section all by themselves over there. Uh-huh. But some strange things happened in the South in those days because I grew up with some Italian kids, and we got to be real good friends. And they were the Rekuparos. And, in fact, their father had a grocery store. And they couldn't -- they could just barely speak English, the father and the mother.

And these kids and I would play together all the time. And one of these kinds, Frankie Rekuparo, we were such close friends as kids until he wanted to go to theater with me, and that was kind of taboo down South in those days. And Frankie -- we were kids, just young kids. And I worked for his father's grocery store delivering groceries. But they would help me deliver the groceries.

By anyway, one day I took Frankie and I put some charcoal dust all over his face -- I never forgot this when he was a little kid -- because he wanted to see a movie that was at the colored theater, the Star Theater at West Broad Street. And this was a picture with Tom Mix in it. I never forgot that. We loved cowboys, you know, in those days.
And so, he wanted to see this movie, and I put this charcoal dust all over his face, and on his hands. But I didn't put any on his neck and his legs. I took him to this

theater, and this old colored fellow -- gentleman -- nice guy. He smiled and he looked at us, and he let us in. I often think about what a bunch of nuts we were at that time. And this was a true story. I never forgot this, you know.
But we thought -- today I look back at it. I see this guy was so wise but he just didn't want to turn us down. He let us go in the theater, you know.
Do you remember the first music you heard in Savannah and what music it was?
Well, you mean in person, or a record, or what?
Well --
We had old gramophones --
Okay, tell me.
-- back in those days.
What is the first music you remember?
The first --
Was it a gramophone or --

Gramophone -- it was -- I'm pretty sure it was Bessie Smith, one of the first ones. Of course, I heard Ma Rainey too, but I think Bessie Smith was about the first one that I heard. But I heard a lot of music in person from the -- these old guitar players because they'd drink a lot, you know, and come in and sing the blues and play these guitars. They'd do that all the whole weekend. Then they'd
go back --
The ones that worked in the turpentine--
Then they'd go back to the turpentine fields.
Do you remember the names of any of them?
No, I don't remember any -- none of them got to be very popular, real popular. But they were good.
Did they make up their own blues, or were they --

Yeah, they'd make their own blues. Most all of them -- most blues singers at that particular time did make up their own blues because there weren't that many blues songs written. There weren't many songs written back in the early 20's, you know, like this was '21, '20, 1919, because I was about seven, eight years old and I was born 1912. So, they weren't -- there wasn't too many blues songs actually written.
Uh-huh.

In fact, in later years some of the guys who could write music would go around and write what a lot of these guys were doing. Got credit for a lot of songs that these old guys made up down there in the fields themselves. Blues was the language of the South back in those days, you know, because they didn't know anything about popular
music, anything like that.

There was some old songs like "Smiles" that came out and songs like that that people used to sing and relate to. In fact, a song I recorded with Luncford (unintelligible) that just got popular as a pop tune when I was a kid down there, that was "Margie", way back then. This must have been around '21, 1920 or '21. The first time I heard it was at a fair-ground. And I always loved music. Whenever I heard it I would try to remember songs, you know.
And there were many old, very old songs back there that people related to back there then. But most -- the biggest thing was blues. That was the biggest thing in the South.

There was a band out of Jacksonville, Florida used to come through there. It was Eagle-Eye Shields band. He has a son today that plays drums around Las Vegas and places like that. And I see him. I often think of his father, you know. But his name was -- he played piano and his name was Eagle-Eye Shields. But he was originally from Savannah, but he went to Jacksonville and he had a good bank together. At --
How big a band?

About six. Bands were -- no bands in those days had over six or seven pieces. If you had eight, nine pieces you had a real big band in those days. But they were five, six pieces -- like that because later on Edmund
Hall played with Eagle-Eye Shields, and so did -- so did Cootie Williams. This is way back.

Edmund Hall was telling me that story how he had to talk to Cootie Williams' mother. Cootie lived in Mobile, and Edmund was from down New Orleans, see, and how he had to talk to his mother to get her -- get them to let Cootie down there and play for him. When I worked with Edmund with Louis he was talking about this story.
And they'd come through there. Joe Oliver would come through Savannah. But Joe Oliver -- when I knew Joe Oliver was coming through there -- Louis wasn't with Joe Oliver at that particular time.
When Joe Oliver came to Savannah that you saw him, what year would that have been? Around what year?
Oh, that would have been before he went to Chicago. That would -- I think he went to Chicago around 1919, 1920 or somewhere around there.
Because it was shortly after that that Barney joined him I know.
Yeah, Barney joined them after that.
So, it was right before then.
And then there was a good band in Savannah. It was called Al Curren and the Snappy Six. That was a real good band that played around Savannah. And there

was a trombone player that played -- I can't think of his name but he went to Europe later. Who played -- I'll think of his name and tell you later, but I can't think of it now. But he played -- in fact, he wrote me from Spain and I sent him a shirt about seven, eight years ago. Aloha shirt to Spain. But he played in -- around New York with Red Allen and quite a few bands. I'll tell you his name when I think of it. I can't think of it right now.
Was there anyone else who came out of Savannah that stayed in music and made any kind of a name?

Later years but I didn't know him them. James Moody came out of Savannah. But I didn't know Moody at that particular time. I guess there are other guys who I really don't know who were musicians in Savannah that came out. There were good musicians all through the South, Atlanta and Savannah. Higginbotham came from Atlanta, J. C. did. He was originally -- he was born down in Georgia (inaudible). Quite a few good guys came from down around in that district, but I didn't know any of them back, there then. You know, I only knew him when he got popular in later years. But I left Savannah in 1926.
So, you were 14.
Yeah, I went to school in Virginia about 40 miles out of -- I had been fooling around with a trombone a little bit around Savannah then. I went to this school
and they had a band there. It was called St. Emma's School, Rock Castle, Virginia, about 40 miles out of Richmond, Virginia. I went there in '26.

In the summers I started in -- started playing in the band around this school. In the summers I would go around Richmond which was 40 miles away. And at that time around Richmond there was a band that was kind of popular, Johnson's Happy Pals. And Roy Johnson and a bunch of them had this band together. They played a lot of blues, and they played a lot of other things. They played dances around there.
So, I'd sit in with them several times. I didn't know too much about what I was doing but I had a lot of fun playing with them, you know, and I learned a lot, you know, around guys like this.

And at that time there was a theater in Richmond in the colored section right around Second and Lee, and this was '26 to '29 around at that time -- called the Hippodrome Theater. And Bessie Smith used to come there a lot. So, I got a chance to really hear Bessie in this theater a couple of times. And I'd go back to school, you know, in September.

I'd work little odd jobs not actually playing music. But in school I took up bricklaying. And so, a guy -- my instructor was from Richmond, Pappa Joe. I don't remember his last name, but anyway, he'd get little jobs for some of us around Richmond. And this was how we picked up a few dollars.

But I'd play a little bit on the side, you know, and I'd go back to school. So, I left this school in '29 and I went to Washington because some guys from the school -- that's when I really started playing in a lot of bands around Washington.

The first band I played in was Booker Coleman's Hot Chocolates around -- this was around Washington, D. C. And I played with Booker Coleman for a while, then I went with Tommy Miles. Tommy Miles Band. Thommy Miles Band had some good musicians in it. Elton Hill was a trumpet player in there, and he was a good arranger. In fact, he arranged some things for Gene Krupa -- Elton Hill -- quite a few things. And Jimmy Mundy was in that band.
I was going to ask you because I noticed that your history and Jimmy Mundy's were rather parallel --
Yeah, he was --
-- for a while there.
Jimmy Mundy was on that band.
You were with Miles' band, and Elmer Calloway -- were you in the band at the same time?
I was in Elmer Calloway's band. Yeah, you're talking about --
Same time with Jimmy Mundy, right?
Yeah, we were in those bands together.
And then you went on to Earl Hines together?

Yeah. Well, what actually happened was we had such good arrangements in that band and some real good players because eventually Eckstine came on that band, and Tyree Glenn came on that band eventually.
Earl Hines band?
No, No. This was Tommy Miles Band.
Tommy Miles Band, oh.
Yeah, and we had some very good musicians in that band.
When did -- you were in Tommy Miles' Band in what year?

It must have been '31, '32 -- '31, '30 because I went with Earl Hines right after that. Jimmy Mundy was the first guy to go with Earl Hines. But I'll tell you how this kind of came about. We used to play a battle of music all the time with a band from Baltimore, and this band was called the Ambassadors.

Now, in this band there was a trumpet player, high note trumpet player. He was very flashy, and his name was Stevenson. But he went with Lunceford later on. He was the first high note trumpet player that Lunceford had before Paul Webster was Stevenson. He went with -- Tommy was a fantastic trumpet player. Played a lot of high
notes. And he was with Lunceford when he got popular in New York at the Cotton Club, Thommy was, and nice looking boy. He was a fantastic trumpet player.

And we used to play a lot of battle of the bands and music with this band. They'd come to Washington. We'd go to Baltimore. And they had some good -- they had a couple of brothers, Chauncey Horton who later played with Cab Calloway. He was on that band. And Shorty Horton, his brother played -- one played the saxophone and one played trombone. And they were very good players on that band.
Was this Miles band or --

This was the other band. This was the Ambassadors from Baltimore. But we had better arrangers -- arrangements than them because we had better arrangers. But I think as a whole, they had better -- more better players than us. On, but we had better arrangements because we had guys -- good arrangers with us. You know, very good arrangers.
Who all was in --

And we had a piano player named Garnett Clark, fantastic little young piano player. He went to Europe years ago. He died in Paris. He was a kind of wild guy. He played with Charlie Barnett for a while way back there then. You know, Charlie was integrated long before anybody else, you know. He went with Charlie -- he went with him way back there then. And there was -- he was amazing piano player. He was a
piano player with Tommy Miles.
How many -- how big a band did Tommy Miles have?
Oh, we had two trombones, we had three trumpets -- that's five -- we had four saxophones -- that's nine -- we had guitar, piano, drums and bass. About 13, 14 pieces.
Do you remember who all else was in the band besides the ones you've mentioned?

That would -- one of the guys his name was Wash Washington. He's a dentist now. He was going to dental school up at Howard University. And he was playing with us. He was an alto player. We had another alto player named Johnny Harris. And Jimmy Munday was the tenor player. And we had another saxophone player, I can't recall now.

And Tommy Miles was the drummer. Garnett Clark was the piano player. I think Chester -- what was Chester's last name -- was a guitar player, because there's another guitar player with the other band, with Booker Coleman, that was Jimmy Owens. He's a fantastic guitar player. He played violin. He died early. And the bass player was Bass Hill, we called him, Pop Hill. He played around New York for a long time. He was on that band on bass.

And the trombones was myself, and another guy named Wendell Jackson from Richmond, Virginia. And the trumpet

players were Warner Carter, Warren Jefferson, and I just can't recall the other trumpet player. But Warren Jefferson went with Earl Hines when I went him, and played lead trumpet with Earl. And he was with Earl, and he didn't stay a real, real long time but he was a good musician. He could range and he could read real well. We had some very good musicians as far as reading and arranging on that band.
When Eckstine came in was it as a singer or as a --

Eckstine came in as a singer. He didn't know how to play a horn at that particular time. So, he was going to Armstrong High School in Washington. And he came in at the Howard Theater in Washington. They used to have an amateur night, I think it was every Wednesday night. I'm not sure of the night.

And the guy who won it would win $50.00. This was a lot of money back then. That was -- man, that was like $5-600.00 now. And the two guys who competed all the time as singers was Billy Eckstine and Bill Kenney, who later on became the lead singer with the Inkspots. And Bill Kenney was from Baltimore. And he became the lead singer.
So, one week Eckstine would win this thing, and another week Kenney -- Bill Kenney would win it.
What determined the winner, the audience applause?

Yeah, the audience applause. And they had other winners too but these guys were pretty consistant on winning it. And Eckstine and I were talking about this -- this band. See, the manager of this band was a guy named Bailey. And Bailey was president of the union, the colored union, because the unions were divided back in those days, you know.

And Bailey used to manage this band. And he'd book us on jobs, and man, he'd tell us, oh, we didn't make much money tonight. He'd give us fifty cents apiece, something like that, and maybe he sold the band, 13 pieces, for $150.00. Fifty cents. We talked about that and we laughed, and everytime I see Eckstine that's a standing joke. Bailey's been dead a long time. Did you see Bailey. You know, did you see Bailey. Ah, yeah, Bailey was -- he was something else, man.

And anyway, Tommy was a nice guy, Tommy Miles. A lot of times we didn't have any money. We were kids and no money to eat with. But Tommy went home, he would have his wife cook up a big pot of beans or something like that. And he'd feed us, you know, over at his house. And we'd rehearse all the time because the guys liked to rehearse.
And we were working on -- we were working on a job there, the Club Prudome. And we must have stayed there about a year, a little longer than a year at that club. And then

we used to play shows at the Howard Theater. We'd go in there, you know, like -- and just play in the pit. We didn't go nothing on the stage because we weren't that good to feature too much on the stage.
Wasn't there a steady house band at the Howard?
We were there. We were a steady house band --
Oh.

-- and another house band I worked with steady there -- I worked in another big band in Washington -- was the Hardy Brothers. That was -- now, that was a good show band. They could -- on the stage they knew how to throw their horns up and down. They did the same routines like Lunceford did, but only this is way before Lunceford. They were doing these kinds of routines way back there then.
What were the Hardy Brothers first names?

Wesley Hardy was one, and I can't think of the other guy's name. Wesley was the thin one, then there's a fat one we called Horse. I never did know Horse's name. But these were the two Hardy Brothers. But they weren't the leaders of the band. The leader of the band was Coleridge Davis, piano player. He led the band and did the arrangements. But it was the Hardy Brothers band, but Coleridge, he seemed
to handle that money and do everything else. He did the hiring and firing, so -- but they use that name, the Hardy Brothers.

And this was a pretty good band. The Hardy Brothers had a pretty good -- not too many of the guys made big names for themselves. But it was a good band. It was a good show, and they were experienced. And we played that circuit of theaters that all the colored bands played then. We called it round the world circuit. Was the Lafayette Theater. This was before the Apollo Theater. Shiffman had another theater called the Lafayette Theater.

And then there was the Alhambra Theater too used to run before the Apollo, right on 125th Street, down the street from the Apollo. And the last one he had was the Apollo. But the first one he had was the Lafayette Theater. This was outside the Lafayette Theater on Seventh Avenue and 131st was what they called the tree of hope.

You'd go out there, you didn't have no job, and rub that tree. You're supposed to get a job. It's kind of absurd when you stop and think of it today.' But this is way back. This is days before I ever got with Earl Hines or any of these bands, and I was playing little bands like that.
In fact, the first band I played in was -- big band -- was Booker Coleman -- I mentioned -- and the Hot Chocolates. And he -- we used to go up to Asbury Park and play all the
summer. There was the hall -- a dance hall up there. I forgot the name of it now, but the guy we played for was Reece Dupree and he was out of Philadelphia.

Well, he didn't pay us nothing much. Once he give us a big sack of potatoes and told us to cook them, you know. We all lived in a big house that he rented. It was Marrow's Hall or something like that in Asbury Park.
Was that your pay -- the sack of potatoes?

Yeah. Well, we get a little bit of money once in a while. But then Father Divine used to come in there, and he would -- he would have a big meeting for three or four nights. And the band went right along with the hall, so we'd make about 50-75¢ apiece the nights when he came there. We made pretty good money there because he was drawing a lot of big crowds, you know.
Father Divine pay you?

All we'd do was open up his set, you know, and play a few songs for him, you know, and get the people coming in, you know. Meeting them, spare a few hymns and let them come on in singing the hymns. That's all we did --
You played the hymns?
Yeah, we played them. We played anything to make some money, man. Things were rough. Yeah, boy. Yeah, I remember those days, man. We played a whole summer
up there. Then we went to Savoy in New York and played a couple of nights up Savoy.
What went on in Father Divine's meetings?

Well, you'd open it up. You'd heat them up with a couple of hot songs. And he'd come out there. You know, he didn't do much himself because he had these guys to preach for him, you know. He had -- he'd go hire the best preachers. These guys down South, man -- pay them good money. He didn't say much. He'd just sit back there and had two pretty girls fan him with the big fans, you know, and he's collecting the money, you know. He had buckets of money, man.
And he didn't do his own preaching? I didn't realize that.

No. Once in a while he'd say a few things but mostly he hired preachers, you know. He'd come out and say a few words, probably the closing words or something. He didn't no hard, no heavy preaching, no. We'd play a couple of nights for him, you know, kind of straight for a while.
That would have been what, about '29 or --
That was about '29, yeah, because I left that band when I went back to Washington and I went with Tommy Miles, see.
Who was in that band?
In Booker Coleman's band?
Uh-huh.

I don't think nobody would know many of the guys, but I'd like to tell you, this was just one trombone, myself. And then we had a trumpet player named Daniel Brashier -- Georgetown we called because he lived in the Georgetown section. And we had another trumpet player from down South, Jake. I can't think of -- he was from North Carolina, but Jake died. And that's what was the brass, two trumpets and a trombone.

Then we had Paul -- Paul Jones played tenor sax. Peter Pole played alto sax. There was another alto man. I can't think of his name. We had three saxes and two trumpets and one trombone. Then we had Jimmy Holmes was the guitar player. And then -- he's the guy I told you who died. He was a left hand guitar player -- violin and guitar. Fantastic player.

But none of them -- Booker Coleman was the leader. He played piano, and he was the leader. And we had a guy named Moody was the drummer. And that was it. We had two trumpets, a trombone, three saxophones, and we had a piano, drums. And that was a big band for those times, you know. And bass. And the bass player's name was Carrington. He was -- lives in Richmond, Virginia now. Carrington. I don't remember his first name. But he was in -- this was Booker Coleman's
band, hot -- first he had a band called the Bellhops, and they wore little bell caps, and little vests like bellmen wear. And I was in on that band, and I wore that stuff once.

Then he changed the name to the Hot Chocolates and he got some almost identical kind of suits where they had brown suits with a stripe down the pants, little vests, and the stripe down the pants, a white shirt, and a brown bow tie. That's all they wore. That was the Hot Chocolates. That was that band, yeah. And he used to travel. We'd go to Norfolk, and Richmond, all the little places around out of Washington, and play, you know.
Did you play mostly dances or --

Oh, that's all we played. Played fairs, and dances, and things like this. Little country fairs and dances. That's all we played, yeah. That's all we played. Most bands then were dance bands. Most all the bands around at that particular time were dance bands. The first show band I ever worked in was that Hardy Brothers band, because Tommy Miles really wasn't a show band. It was more of a swing and dance band, you know.

It was on the style of Earl Hines Band. It was similar to that because the arrangers, that's the way they wrote. And they went in Earl's -- Mundy went with Earl and he wrote the same way. And he with -- he went with Goodman later on and some of the songs that Goodman played we used to
play around Washington. It got popular. That "Swingtime in the Rockies", that was called the "Chocolate Stomp". We used to play that around Washington all the time.
You mean it was called the "Chocolate Stomp" first?
Oh, yeah, before Goodman ever heard it.
Goodman heard it and just changed the name.
Well, he made the arrangement. Mundy changed the name. He made the arrangement for Goodman, and he changed the name himself. And he got credit for the tune. And it really wasn't his tune.
Anybody know who wrote it or --
We made it up.
The band?

A bunch of us got together and made it up, you know. It was called head arrangements. That's what we called those that we made up. And, in fact, that's all Basie used to play at first. You know, he had arrangements. They didn't -- when he left Kansas City they didn't have hardly nothing written. They were doing head arrangements, but they were good because they set down and worked it out the way they were going to do it. They would have rehearsals and say let's do this here, that there. And different guys would say, well, maybe next chorus we'll do this or that. Behind so and
so's solo we'll do this-- (End of Tape One)
You were talking about when Basie left Kansas City and the kind of music he had, head arrangements.

Yeah, that's right. They were all head arrangements, you know, but they were good arrangements, as I said before. You know, because they sat down and worked these things out. It wasn't just like getting up on the stand guessing about what they were doing. They sat down at rehearsals and worked them out, the tempos and everything.
Which is the way the bands that you were with did, right?

Well, most of the ones I was with, except for Booker Coleman and the Hot Chocolates, they were written arrangements. Tommy Miles and all -- almost everything Tommy Miles had was -- they were written arrangements. Naturally you made up a few things, you know, but most of the things were written because he had -- he had an abundance of good arrangers over there, you know, Tommy Miles did. He couldn't write himself but he had several arrangers in that band.
He had Jimmy Mundy and --

Elton Hill, Warren Jefferson, Warner Carter, trumpet player. He had about five or six. A piano player used to be with the band, he wrote -- Garnett Clark, the young guy I mentioned. And he had about six or seven real pretty good
arrangers.
When did you start arranging?

I never did too much arranging myself. I composed, but I never did too much arranging. But I -- I was more of a composer then than arranger. I wrote -- I started writing tunes I guess way back because some of the tunes that I had written I never do anything with them until later. But when I went with Earl Hines, one of the tunes that I had written, Charlie Carpenter wrote the -- I don't know if you knew Charlie.
Yeah.

He wrote the lyrics for -- and Charlies was band boy with Earl Hines back there in those days. He and another little guy named Dunlop and I wrote -- the first thing I wrote was "A Lover is Blue". And Tommy Dorsey recorded it. And that's when Jack Leonard sang with Tommy Dorsey. And Tommy recorded it. And the next thing I wrote was "Traveling Light", and almost lost that tune because I went up to Jimmy Mundy, and he said he was going to make an arrangement on it, you know.

And I went up to his house. He lived in New York then. And I was with Earl Hines. And I showed him I went. And he -- I didn't even know he made an arrangement on it. He was writing for Whiteman back there then. And he made an arrangement on it. And the story I got was somebody asked him

whose tune was that, and he said it was his tune.

So then, Johnny Mercer wrote lyrics for it. And the record came out and my name wasn't on it. So, I got so angry about it because all the guys knew it was my tune, but I didn't have sense enough to copyright it. So, you know, but I knew I could prove it was my tune. But that's finally when my name got on the tune. So, I had to blame Munday for not telling them it was my tune.

I didn't mind if he had cut himself in on it, said it was he and mine. But to leave me completely out of, I felt -- I felt hurt about it. And I never did really kind of get over that but I don't hold it against him because of the fact that we were friends. You just don't do that to a friend of yours, you know. This is -- Budd Johnson knows the whole story because Budd was with Earl back then at that time.
Well, when did you finally get your name on the record?

Oh, well, I missed all of the royalties from the first record because my name wasn't on it then and -- from the first months of that Billie Holiday record. And that was the most lucrative part of it, you know. I got it all later, about a year or so later.
Because I know in her book she says that you each got $75.00.
Yeah, that's right.
And that neither one of you ever saw Levit. another thing.

No, we didn't. And this -- when her book came out I hadn't gotten anything else from it at that time. But, you know, it was -- I felt bad about it because, you know, if somebody do that to do and you don't know him, you don't feel so bad. But for a friend, you know, a guy that you consider a friend -- because I was his best man at his wedding, you know, when he married his first wife, Dorothy, you know.

In fact, when she died later -- years later, after all this problem happened, I went out -- myself and Louis Taylor, another trombone player, and we played a song with organ for -- at her funeral, you know. But you know, I couldn't hold it against her. She didn't do nothing to me, you know. But these things happen in this business, you know.
But you had been working with him though for so long.
Yeah, we were friends, but that's part of the business I guess, you know.
Back in Savannah --
Yeah.
-- how did you happen to start playing trombone. You said you had fooled around a little bit in Savannah before you --

Yeah, well, I knew -- I knew a few musicians around Savannah and they played instruments. And they didn't play them very well but they played them, you know. And I used to hang around some of these musicians. I was just a kid.

And they'd let you pick up their horn and fool around with it, you know. And there was a guy down there, Georgia Red, he's a trombone player. And I used to fool -- he didn't play very good. But he lived in my neighborhood. So -- and he'd come around there. And we had a piano at my house. And a couple of guys played piano pretty good. My sister used to study piano. Came around there and they would play and eat. Some of them with their instruments would get right there and fool around with their instruments.

But there were really not many good players around there. The best musicians around Savannah at that time to me were the old blues players that didn't know anything about what they were doing, but they played. You know, they didn't -- as far as knowing, they didn't know what they were doing. But it sounded good. They had a knack for doing what -- and the blues players then were far ahead of other players back at that time. You know, because it was their own thing, you know. They weren't copying nobody, just how they felt, And they were expressing their feelings.
Is the trombone the first instrument you
I fooled around with trumpet a while. It just got a little too rough for me. And I fooled around with drums a little while but --
At what age?

Oh, I was just a kid. I was -- I guess I was 15, 14, 15. When I first left Savannah I fooled around with so many instruments. But around Savannah I had picked up a trumpet and fooled around with that a lot, more than I did with trombone. And I didn't own any instrument.

Then I used to fool around -- there was a guy named Freddie Slee had drums, and I used to fool around with his drums. And he was a pretty bad drummer too. He couldn't play good. But he had drums, you know.
Do you remember how old you were when you first started fooling around with the trumpet?

Yeah, I guess I was about 12. Because the first time I really did get around with a trombone where I would fool around with it all day and things like this was when I first went to that school in 1926. I had messed around. I could play a little blues on trombone. I had worked out a little bit of blues but I didn't know too much about it. I didn't know anything about what I was doing.
So, you sort of taught yourself?
Yeah. At first, yeah. I took lessons
later, in later years.
I saw in Chilton's book that you had an uncle who played trombone in Jim Europe's band. Was he any kind of an influence on you, or did he have anything to do with your--

No, he didn't have any. He played but he didn't influence me. Who influenced me for trombone was these guys in the Jenkin's Orphan Band. They were the guys who really influenced me because I'd watched them. In fact, I think I liked the way they walked, you know. That was the first thing. And they's slide those horns all out--. They had a lot of color with what they were doing and this influenced me an awful lot.

And besides the fact that I liked the sound of the trombone. I don't think -- I didn't think I could ever learn the trumpet. It just seemed much harder to me, you know, at that time being a kid, you know. But I wanted to play trumpet first but it just seemed so hard to me. And then after I heard Louis play, from then on I said I don't think I could ever do that, you know. And he was playing so good so far back there then, you know. He was amazing because he was so far ahead of his time.
And after I had heard all the other trumpet players in Jenkin's Orphan Bandand all, then finally I heard Louis. And well, this was the epitome to me -- I think to almost all
musicians back in the '20's. Louis was just it, you know.
Was the Jenkins Orphan Band very, very young players, or were they --
Yeah, they were young. They were young boys.
But they were still like minors --
Yeah, they were ---
(inaudible).
Oh, yeah. But they could play because --
How old -- from what age range --

I think -- I think they ranged from about 13 to about -- 13 or 14 to about 18. I think they were about in that bracket, you know. But they were always training younger ones to come up, you know. They were very young.
You said your sister studied piano. How many children were there in your family?
Well, I had some half brothers, and then I had three sisters and some half brothers. I have two sisters living now. My half brothers are dead.
And did your sister study -- one sister studied piano?
Just one, yeah.
And you started with trumpet and went to trombone. Was there anybody else in the family who played a --
No, there's this uncle who I didn't really know real well. He was -- played trombone.
What was his name?
His name was Will.
Young?

Uh-huh. I didn't know him real -- I didn't know him real well. I didn't know too much about him because -- you know, most of the people in Savannah, they left and went to New York. Most of the people in New Orleans, they went to Chicago. I guess there was a direct line from both spots, you know, but most all people from Savannah went to New York. There are more people from -- right today, their roots were in Savannah. They will live in New York.
I didn't realize that --
Yeah.
-- there was a direct move.
And just like most people from Louisiana go to Chicago back at that time, it seems. It's probably the way the trains ran or something like that -- a direct line, see.
What were your parents names?
My mother's name was Annie, and my father's name was the same as mine. But they didn't call me junior. (Laughter)
What did they call you?

He used to call me James. You know, most of them down there call me that. James O. My father called me James O. My mother did. Most of my friends called me James or Jim, you know, Jimmy. But I didn't get that name "Trummy" until later years around Washington. And this guy Booker Coleman named me that.

But how we got that name is he couldn't remember names. So, he called the bass player Bassie, and he called the drummer Drumski, and he called me Trummy. And just my name just stuck. That Trummy just stuck. But he'd call everybody, you know, Trumpski -- the trumpet player -- that's because he couldn't remember names. It wasn't because he was trying to give me any name. But that name just stuck on me, you know.
But in Chilton's book he says Tommy Miles gave you that name.
No.
It wasn't Tommy Miles?
No.
Booker Coleman.
Booker Coleman gave me that name. He was wrong.
And it stuck for good because I notice on --
Before I went with Tommy. Booker --
So, you already had it when --
Yeah, Booker named me that.
But I notice on some of the Lunceford record labels it has "Bobo" by Jimmy Young.

No, they made a mistake. They put Johnny Young on one. The first, the very first record I made of "Margie". The guy They asked me, you know, being from the South I don't guess you talk very clearly. So, he asked me my name. I said Trummy Young. So, maybe Trummy sounded like Johnny to him, you know, because I remember the original, the first record I made of "Margie" with Lunceford it had Johnny Young on it.
Well, I -- I don't think I have that one but I have some that say -- you look at the trombones and it has James Young on trombone, but --
Yeah.
-- there's a vocal by Jimmy Young.
Yeah, I guess so. I guess --
Did they ever call you Jimmy?

No, not since I've been -- not since I've played professionally. Everybody called me Trummy. In fact, a lot of them didn't know my name was James. Lot of people -- and they don't even know it today, a lot of people don't, you know. Because that name, it's been on me so long. Because I've had people say how did you ever get a name like that, and then
when I explain to them it's from the trombone, they say oh, we never thought of that, you know. Strange isn't it, you know. They say we never thought of that, you know.
When did you decide that you would want to be a professional musician, professional trombone player?

All my life I wanted to be a professional. But I used to whistle all day long before I ever played any instrument, you know. Down in Savannah I was forever whistling, you know. I just love music. I never did want to do anything else before I ever played music, you know.

And one reason -- I tell you, when I went to that school, I knew I was going to play music. Because this was a military school, and I saw these guys out there with rifles drilling in that sun and the band was sitting up underneath some trees playing. I said now I know I want to be a musician, you know, because I didn't want to go through that, man. I knew darn well then that I wanted to be a musician.

But I wanted to be. That wasn't the main reason. That was one good reason. The -- it wasn't the main reason I wanted to. I just love music, you know. And I was supposed to have been a bricklayer around that school, and everytime they had to find me I was around the bandroom. They couldn't keep me out of that bandroom. I couldn't play nothing but the blues, but, you know, everybody from the South then could play the blues because
that's all you heard all day long.
But you got instruction, formal music instruction at that school or did you just play with --

You play marches (unintelligible). We used to jazz up the marches sometime. They'd get after us and tell us to tone it down. We'd try to put some jazz notes in the marches. But we'd play a few overtures, things like the William Tell Overture, a few things. But mostly it was march. It was march music. When we were on our own, we'd try anything with those instruments, you know.

Just experimenting around, of course. The guy who taught us, his name was John Scott. And he was from Richmond, Virginia. Big, tall, nice looking brown-skinned guy. And he was the teacher, but he taught all the instruments. And he really didn't know all the instruments that well but he taught us to the best of his ability. His instrument, I think, was clarinet. Naturally the clarinet players got a better musical education than the rest of us did. But we had a lot of fun playing.

We'd just get together and anything we heard we try to play it. March, or any kind of thing, you know. If we heard an operatic singer we'd try to play what they were singing. It was just a challenge to us to play things, you know. Half of us didn't -- never knew what key we were in. We were just fooling around.

In fact I never really took a trombone lesson from a good trombone teacher until I got with Earl Hines. I never did really take an interest in really getting to the foundation, the basics of it. And then once I started it was hard to stop because it was like a new world to me, something I really enjoyed doing, you know.

I'll never forget what made me do it was I was playing with two trombone players who had studied with Earl Hines. And it was Billy Franklin and Louis Taylor. And Louis Taylor had studied with a Polish gentleman in Chicago. His name was Jerry -- Gerislav Shimera (PHONETIC) And he lived way out in Oak Park in Chicago. So, it was a long subway ride. I lived on the South Side and that was a long -- about a 45 minute ride out on -- all the way out to Jerry's home.

And when I first went out there he asked me to play a B flat scale for him. So, I think it was so horrible, what I played was so bad until -- he asked me where did I work. So, I told him. He said you get paid for playing. So, I told him yeah. He shook his head, you know. He wondered how, you know, because -- well, I could play jazz. I really had no -- I didn't know nothing about intonation. I didn't know anything about it.
And these two guys did. So, they said, look, if you're going to play with us you got to work on your tone, and you got to do this and that. And, you know, but I never

worried about that. I had a hard enough time playing the notes, you know. So after working in Tommy Miles' band we never did -- intonation wasn't one of our strong points. Let's put it that way, you know.

But these guys were more professional, you know, who were playing in that band. And there were some good guys in that band. So, I worked hard. I went out to this teacher, and he showed me what to do. And I'll never forget. He was charging $2.00 a lesson back there then. That was a lot of money, you know, back there then because when I first went with Earl, I think I was making about oh, $40-45.00 a week, you know. And that was a lot of money, $2.00.

Anyway, so -- I stayed -- I went to this man and I got carried away. I was intrigued. I didn't know that all these things went on with the trombone. So -- and I'd go from week -- every week I'd go. I worked hard at it. And he was a funny man. He told me, he says if you don't study, don't come back next week. I don't -- I'm not looking for students, he said, because I can get all the students I want.

At the same time I was going to him some top trombone players in some of the top bands were studying with him. Tommy Peterson was studying with him at that time. So was Eddie Cosby. Eddie Cosby's name is Eddie Cosboski, but he changed it to Eddie Cosby. But we all were studying with him at that time, and I didn't know they were going to turn out to
be top trombone players. And they didn't know it was going to happen to me.

But he was a very meticulous man. He didn't care who you were. If you were serious about it he would help you. Because after he found out I was serious he told me, look, if you don't have any money come out anyway and take your lesson. Because -- and he paid me a high compliment later on in later years. He said I was the most apt student that he ever had. You know, it really made me feel good because he had some really fantastic trombone players that studied with him. I felt it was a great honor for him to have mentioned that about me.

But, you know, back in those days when I came along, it isn't like today where kids, they learn about tone -- intonation and all this before they even get the instruments they learn. There was no road to go on. We had to make our own road for the kids, you know, today, back there in those days. Really because all a trombone player did back then was -- (imitates a trombone). That's the only way they played. They didn't know any other way to play.

In fact, the first trombone player I ever heard in my life that didn't play like that was a guy called I think it was Arthur Prior. He was a band -- it wasn't a jazz band -- he was a band master, you know. And he played all these intricate parts in a band. And I said, wow, I sure want to play like that, you know. And I don't want to play all this
[handwritten musical notation]
(imitates a trombone) on the thing. You know, I wanted to really play some nice things like I heard this guy play.

And I started working more on playing things like this, and this is what made me pick up in jazz before I ever got a lesson because I wanted to get around a little bit on the horn and do some different things than what I had been hearing.

And when I first started -- when I first went with Earl a lot of people thought I was nuts, some of the things I was playing because guys just weren't playing those kind of things at that particular time, you know. But to me it was a challenge to play. I figured the trumpets and all were playing like that. Why couldn't the trombones play like that way back there then.

So, it was just a different thing altogether. And trombone players didn't play real high anything like that back at that time, and I loved to play high. You know, I was just getting into it. I made a lot of bad notes trying to do it because I remember once, Stanley Dance's wife now --
Helen Oakley, (inaudible) writing for Downbeat.
Yeah. She was just starting (unintelligible).

And Benny Goodman was in -- Benny Goodman was in Chicago playing at the Congress Hotel. He's just getting started too. And I was with Earl Hines over at the Grand Terrace. And I'd take all kind of chances. I tried anything

I thought of -- I just tried. And naturally, it all ain't going to come out. So, I guess she came there one of those nights when it wasn't working, and she -- she wrote an article in Downbeat and said the trombone player was atrocious. And she probably was right, you know. I had to laugh about that thing, but it hurt me so bad at that time until I think I started practicing about eight hours a day after she wrote that.

I really went to practicing then. I said I'm not going to let this chick write like -- about me like that. And I just really. So, Earl and Stanley, they kid Helen when they want to kid her now. They say oh don't say nothing. You're the one that put Trummy down (unintelligible). And we were laughing about that a few days ago out there at Colorado, you know.

I said, well, Helen, you were right. I was kind of bad because I was just experimenting. And it happens to a guy who's taking chances. It's going to happen to you. It's like a ball player, you know. The guys who make the most errors are the guys who take the greatest chances. You're going to make errors if you take chances. But I was that kind. I was a gambler, you know, with that horn. I just took chances.
Some things I know I had no business trying. But -- because my technique wasn't up to what my ideas were at that particular time. But it just made me work harder to try to get
enough technique to do those things that I was attempting to do back there then.
Where was it that you saw Arthur Prior or heard Arthur Prior?

I heard him in the band concert in Washington, D. C. Yeah, that's where I heard him. And I heard him at a band concert before that in Richmond, Virginia, in the '20's, about '28. And he didn't play -- he couldn't play any jazz. And he couldn't do a lot of little tricks that I had learned to do -- jazz things, but I liked what he was doing, you know. He could play. He could -- he had command of the instruments, you know. And this is what I wanted to do, you know, back there then.

And, you know, all the time I went to that school I was trying to work on things like that. I continued to do it when I left there. I left there in 1930 and that's when I went to Washington, D. C. And that's the first time I ever bought a trombone. I bought my own horn. I got -- I bought a horn in a pawn shop then in Washington. I had the things in a cloth -- I used to -- took a sheet and cut it around the trombone because I didn't have no case. And I made that sheet to fit around it. I had to be very careful I didn't hit the slide and dent it.
I used to have the worse slides and it was hard to pull them because I'd dent them. I didn't know too much about
caring for slides and things in those days. In fact, I was talking out to the factory here today -- the other day -- Olds Factory.

There was a little guy who worked out there named Benny years ago. He was crippled. That's when Olds Factory was -- this was '32, somewhere around that time. It was on Raymond Street. And he knew so much about slides. He worked on horns. I was talkin to He's dead now. The top machinist -- one of the top machinists out at Olds Factory now And he said Benny taught him. And he said, yeah, I remember Benny. Benny was the guy who taught me. I said, well, Benny was the guy who showed me -- the first -- the first guy that showed me how to take care of a slide.

I didn't -- I just played. I didn't know anything about taking care of the thing or anything. I just played it and that was it. When we came up we didn't -- you know, we didn't know anything about things like that. So, I teach kids today about horns. And the average kid playing the horn, they don't know really the proper care for a horn, how You should keep the horn clean and -- because I didn't know it. I try to help kids today.

And all the guys I knew, they were too busy to help us when I came long as kids. This guy was a fantastic trombone player in the '20's with Fletcher Henderson. And he played at Small's Paradise before -- Jimmy Harrison. He could play

but he was drunk all the time, you know. And so, you'd go ask him something about a horn. Get away from here, kid, can't you see I'm busy. He had chicks and all, but that's why I can never turn a kid down today because I think of those things. And actually, the guy probably know too much to tell me anyway because they really didn't know. You know, they hadn't made a scientific study of it. They really just didn't know. He couldn't have -- probably couldn't have told me.

In later years I found out that -- I would look for guys who knew these things and there weren't too many trombone players who know them. Even when I came long with -- Jack Teagarden and myself -- we always used to jam a lot and get together. Brunis and Jack and myself, and we'd run in together. Sit around -- Higginbotham -- we'd jam.

But they didn't -- some of their horns were so dirty. You'd be surprised, man. You'd run water through there -- roaches, anything liable to jump out of that horn, you know. But they didn't know. They didn't know about -- everybody drank a lot. You wasn't making no money. So, you'd try to have some fun.

You know, we used to blow all night, and one of the things that I think helped most of us were we were constantly playing. We didn't make anything but we'd go out after work and play all night. The only time we weren't playing was probably when we were asleep.
Uh-huh.

But nobody plays that much any more. You don't have those training grounds. You don't have those sessions. We didn't make nothing going on a jam session in those days. Where they were -- it didn't have to be in a club. It could be in somebody's basement, any place -- where we used to have those things. Just get guys and get together.

If a guy came in town, he could play -- well, everybody was after this guy, you know. Man, let's try to catch old so and so. And they was trying to catch him if he could play, you know. They'd invite him, come out, man, you know. And everybody'd get up there and take shots at him. You know, some of them we could handle and some of them we couldn't.

But every time you're sharpening your knife -- you're sharpening your knife all the time. Everytime you do that you're sharpening up, see. And this is what we did back there then in those days.
Where was it that you used to all get together. Was it anytime you ran into each other on the road or --

Anywhere. On the road. I remember one day we were in Oklahoma City, and we were playing Oklahoma City. So, we were in a little club. I was with Lunceford and we heard this guitar player. Man, he was playing so much. So, Eddie Durham was with Lunceford's band.

So, the guys went and told Eddie Durham. Say, Eddie, there's guitar player around here, but anyway he don't play so good, you know. Eddie Durham was playing (unintelligible) trombone and guitar. It's the kind of tricks guys used to play. So, he went around to this little club, and it was Charlie Christian.
(Laughter)

Eddie Durham wanted to beat up all those guys. But these are the little kind of tricks that guys used to play on one another, you know. Like -- and around New York especially, you know. But all the cities had it. It was going on in all the cities. But there were places around New York, them guys had little basements. They used to sell liquor. It wasn't -- it was illegal, you know. And they'd have certain nights, certain instruments play. Like maybe one night it would be nothing but pianos. Piano players.
Like at Mexico's in New York?
Yeah, this is the way it used to be way back. But they had several spots like that around.
Oh, really, where? I only know about Mexico's, Maxico's.

There was one on 131st Street, and there was the 101 Ranch. They used to have shows there but after they shows they just -- there were a lot of little spots. Over at the Elks Club on Lenox Avenue, there was several little clubs used to do it. One night there wouldn't be nothing but

tap dancers over there, dancing against one another, you know. There was all kind of different things they had going, you know. Whoever was in town, you know, they would get together. Sometimes you'd go by some guy's apartment that had a piano, and you just get in there and jam, you know. A lot of them are private that nobody even know but the guys who were playing about them -- knew about this. But Mexico, yeah he had his place. Maxie (inaudible).

And then there was the Rythmn Club there. A lot of guys, all the musicians used to hang out around there. If a top act would come in town -- well, everybody's laying for them, you know. Yeah, these things happened all over New York, and they used to have them all over Chicago.

I remember when we were in Chicago we used to go out at the Delisa Club. This is the old Mike DeLisa's club. Was on the other side of the street. This is when Albert Ammons had a band. And the guy in there, Guy Kelly was on trumpet in the band, and Albert Ammons and this guy Kelly, and Israel Crosby was on bass. I forgot who was on the drums.
But they had a little band in there. And Leon Washington -- Goon was on tenor sax. And why, we all used to go in there and jam. Every night. And Roy was playing with Fletcher then, Roy Eldridge.
What year would this have been?
This would be around '33, '34. Roy was playing with Fletcher, so was Chu Berry. And Higgy was with--
Higginbotham,
Higginbotham. But we used to all go over there and jam over there and --
At the DeLisa?

Yeah, and we'd jam all night over there, yeah. Things -- these things went on up to the -- about the early '40's. That's when they start slacking off. Well, the union started tightening up on it because a lot of guys, they wouldn't even hire any musicians and yet they could get all that music for nothing. And they were doing fantastic business. So, the union moved in. And, of course, I don't know. One thing Led to another.

Up at Minton's -- used to go at Minton's. Same thing. But even before modern jazz got up at Minton's, they used to run the sessions up there. A lot of guys used to go. I used to go up there and play a lot. But all over. They had these things on 52nd Street, all around. But way before 52nd Street these things because -- and Monroe's Uptown House -- they used to -- that was all they did up there was jam all the time.

I've heard that some of the major horn players used to carry their own rhythm sections with them for sessions. They'd go out after work and challenge somebody, but they'd bring along their own rhythm.
Yeah, they used to do that. A lot of them used to do that.
Do you remember who? I understand
Ben Webster had his own, and who else?
Well, before Ben --
Coleman Hawkins -- (Unintelligible). Hawk used this (unintelligible) is before Ben, and Blanche Calloway. Guys were doing that around New York.
Do you remember who and who they had with them?

Well, I don't remember exactly who was with him but they would -- especially they would have their own bass and piano player with them. It probably would be whoever they were working with at that particular time because the guys knew what they were playing, you know. For instance, if I'm working in say a little band on 52nd Street every night, well, they'd get into what I was playing. If I went out to jam, I could take them out with me. I'd say come on, let's go over to so and so place and play. This was just like taking your own group with you almost.
Uh-huh.

In his room?
He'd rent, you know, yeah. Bring it up

And Chicago was alive in those days. I remember we played a show at the Oriental Theater with Earl Hines, and that show was Milton Berle. But nobody knew much about him then. Did he and Earl every play the same place, the same time. I mean like late after hours.
Not that I can recall but I imagine they

did because they both were very proud guys, you know. They both could play, you know. So, I imagine they did. I know Tatum -- anywhere a piano player was, he'd go, you know. He was like a lion, man, a roaring lion. This was his cup of tea, you know. He would do it all -- I don't care where a piano player was, he would go. He'd find him, you know. I lived in a -- in later years I lived in an apartment building out in Los Angeles where Tatum lived. And he had a piano up there. And he'd play all day. West side?

Uh-huh.

You know, Joe Louis used to stay on St. Andrews.
Joe lived there.

That's where he lived.

Who else was in it?

In Lips' band? I don't remember. I really don't remember but he had a good band. Sandy was on that band. It was a good little band he had. And then I worked in 52nd Street with Tiny Grimes had a little band. And

And I had a ball playing for her. I couldn't get out of the room because Art Tatum was coming on after her, you know. I just went to the john and that was about it, man, and I came back on. Good drummer.

But we backed her, you know. And Tiny had the gig. It was Tiny's gig. You know, in those days it didn't matter who the leader was. Whoever got the gig, he was the leader, man. You know, that was it, you know. And he had the gig. And he might leave right out of there and another guy get a gig, and Tiny be playing the guy's band -- one of the guys who was in that band. That's how things always worked back there then, you know.
Yeah, we had a lot of fun though down there. But when I left Earl, I went to New York then to join Lunceford. And
when I went in with Lunceford's band, there was two of us went in there together. Saxophone player named Teddy Buckner from Detroit, Milt Buckner's brother.
A saxophone player named Teddy Buckner?
That's right.
Was it Teddy Buckner that plays now? trumpet near
Ted Buckner -- no, it was a saxophone player, Milt Buckner's brother. Milt Buckner, the piano and organ player used to play with Hamp. They were from Detroit. No relation to this Teddy Buckner.
Oh.

Here. But he was a fine alto man. In fact, he was -- played the alto chorus on "Margie", the very first chorus. And Willie Smith always got credit for -- and Buckner used to feel so bad. But we went in that band together. I never forgot that. It was September, '37. And we rehearsed about two, three weeks in New York before we ever went out on a job with that band. And right after that we came right back and made "Margie, the record "Margie". "Annie Laurie" and "Margie" and some other things -- right after that. Right -- and I never
did do any singing in no band before. I never sang, you know, with Earl or anybody.

But one day I was singing that -- singing "Margie" on the train, and Sy heard it. Sy -- he said, wow. He said, why don't you sing that. I said, oh, I don't -- I never did any singing. He said, but that would be good. He said, sing that again for me. So, I sang it and he wrote down exactly how I was singing it. He had me sing it over and over the way I was singing it.

He said, you know what I'm going to do? He said, I'm going to write a background that fit the vocal -- behind the vocal. But he wrote the vocal first, and this is one of the few times anybody ever did that -- wrote the way a guy sang a song -- the vocal, and then made the background fit the vocal. That's why the reeds can answer it so good because he knew exactly what I was singing. And we did this on the train.

He got his pad out and his paper and right on the train one day. I never forgot that. We were going, I think, from Philadelphia to Washington. And he made -- he sketched it out on the train. So, he says, you know, you're singing in the key of D. You're singing -- I said, I don't sing. I told you I'm not a singer. I'm just fooling around with this things. And he wrote it out in the key of D which is a pretty rough key because most guys didn't play and sing in that key back there then, you know. And this is how we got
that thing to going.

And later on he and I became very close friends. We became roommates on that band. And so, one Sunday we were in Nashville and I was humming a little thing that I used to always hum around Chicago. You know, we used to sneak out drinking in Chicago when I was with Earl. And liquor wasn't legal then, you know, back there then, you know.

So, this guy used to serve liquor in teacups. And we used to -- I used to always kid him about it. His name was Ike. So, I made up a little thing. (Sings) "The--taint what'cha do--way h'atcha do it" (unintelligible) and a little thing like -- we used to kid him. So, Sy heard me humming that one day and he said, let's make a song out of that. I said ok. So, one sunday in Nashville we weren't working, and he and I sat down -- there was a piano in the lady's house and we got fooling around with it. And that's when we made up that tune "It taint what you do, it's the way how you do it." (up-to-date)
Oh.

One Sunday out in Nashville. He and I wrote several little things together then. I left the -- he left the band. I started writing a few little things on my own, and I -- the first thing I wrote when he left was "What's you know, Joe", that little tune. I used to like to write little catchy phrases like that, you know. I did another song for Billie Holiday just before she died but -- and she liked it

but she wasn't in no shape to sing it then. And I've never done anything with the tune since. I wrote it with a guy in Honolulu there, Andy Cummings. But maybe later on I'll try to do something. It's called "Riff-raff", you know. Cute little tune but we never did -- she liked it but she was in no shape then when I last saw her.
But I used to like to write. I did a lot of composition.
What are your other? I mean I guess I know--
"Travlin Light"

But the best -- I think the best thing I ever did was that "Traveling Light". I think it's the best thing I ever did. I didn't write the lyrics for it but I liked the melody.

couldn't. I haven't been back into writing but I want to get back into it now.
You should,

Yeah, I want to. I really want to get back. But with Lunceford I had a lot of incentive to do things because everybody over there was on their toes and trying to do something, you know. you decided the arrangement of "Margie" did you record it? How long after (inaudible).

We recorded it before we ever did play it out anywhere on a job.

Most guys liked to play a tune out on a job about a week or so before they recorded it, but we never did record that -- play that out on a job before we recorded it. I think we did that for Decca. I'm pretty sure we did when I was with
him. But we did that -- we did a lot -- we did a lot of tunes then for Decca, then he did a lot for Columbia later on, Lunceford did.

But I don't know. I enjoyed recording with that band because they worked hard. They got the song right, you know, before they would really record it. And it was a good recording band. That's something you have to work at, recording. A lot of bands play good, don't record good. And that's a -- that's strange, isn't it.

But I'll tell you another good recording band to me back there then was Andy Kirk. I thought he had a fine recording band especially when he had Pha Terrell singing with him like -- things like "Until the Real Thing Comes Along" and things of that sort. The band sounded mellow, you know, really caught on in the studios.

Oh, Lunceford, we did a lot of good -- we did so many one-nighters though, Whew. You know, we did more one-nighters than I think than anybody. Yeah, Lunceford's band. We -- sometimes we'd do 90 or more in a row, you know. Just -- you'd be so dead when you left, so tired, and so glad to get a day off or something like that because it was rough, you know. You couldn't get decent food, and traveling.
I remember one night we were going somewhere down Florida. And we got through a job and we got -- we couldn't go nowhere to eat. So, Will X Smith, he looks white anyway.

So, we sent him in a place. Sure enough, he got a lot of sandwiches for us, about $30.00 worth of sandwiches. But we couldn't go into the place. So, you know, he went in and got it. Things were that bad back there then. You know, New York was even bad. You know the story --
(inaudible).
Oh, yeah. At one time. I mean not that bad but, you know, when Billy ie Holiday was singing with Artie Shaw they wanted her to come in the back door, you know.
Yeah, right. But that was mixing (inaudible).
But when -- so long as people kept separate, there was a place to get something to eat, wasn't there?
You could eat. New York wasn't that bad but it had its bad points. It wasn't as bad as that South was down there. Things were kind of rugged, you know.
Willie had a sort of strange dual-existance.
He sure did.
He could go in and get food --

Yeah, but he had a problem down South when he played down South because once a policeman once told him come off that bandstand. He said, you can't be playing with them. You come off that stand. But he had to carry his birth certificate around with him. That's the only way we could -- he could get to play with us.

I know Willie used to tell stories about when he was with Harry James, and how they would -- advance word would get to these other cities that Harry James had a mixed band. There was one Negro in the band. And so, the sheriff would come up and say to Harry James you can't go on with a mixed band. And Harry would say, all right, point out the one that mixes it.
Yeah.
And nobody -- I mean --
No, they couldn't tell.

Who could tell looking at Willie. And so -- and other times Harry James would be told he couldn't go on if he let Willie play. And so, Harry James would walk away and not play the date. But on the other hand, it was a convenience when you couldn't get food.

Oh, yeah. Barnett had a lot of problems over -- when we used to play with Barnett. We didn't go way down South. We'd be in places like West Virginia, you know. And he'd have a problem. I remember once with Benny Goodman, it was Teddy, Slam and myself, we had a problem in Providence in a hotel.
What happened?
Well, they didn't want us. So, Teddy approached Benny. He says -- he said, we have a problem here. We can't get a room in the hotel. He said, we though you made

a reservation. Benny said -- then he says they don't want to let us have a room. So, Benny didn't go to the front for this, you know. He said you know I have problems too. I can't belong to this Jewish club, this club or that one because I'm Jewish.
So, we told him we was going back to New York. We told him thanks very much but we were going -- we didn't have to go through that. Then he got something done about it when we told him that.
Personally, did he -- (inaudible)
No, he went and got somebody else to do something about it.
That's what I wondered. I mean I've heard so many Benny Goodman stories.

Yeah, he didn't. But I don't know. He's strange anyway, you know. You got a strange person, you know. But he wouldn't battle those things out. But that's one thing I can say about Charlie. He would fight, man. He would. And so would Boyd Raeburn. I played with Boyd Raeburn's band, you know. And Boyd was a beautiful cat -- did you ever know him?
No, I never did. I know he had a great band but --
He was a beautiful cat, man. He'd fight. You know, he would -- he'd say, well, they don't stay here, none of us stay here, you know. That was his way, you know.

But I guess everybody wasn't like that, you know. I liked Benny, you know, but I don't think Benny would go too far for nobody. Not only us but nobody else, you know. He didn't think like that. He just thought clarinet and that was it, you know.
Yeah.
Great, great player. The guy's a great player but that's what he -- the way he thought was strictly clarinet. He didn't let anything else bother him. Clarinet was it, man, you know.
Where all did Boyd Raeburn's band tour?
Huh?
Where all did Boy Raeburn's band tour?

Well, we toured New England, and we toured Jersey. We didn't go too far. We'd play around West Virginia and Washington, D. C. It used to be a kind of problem around there, you know. And near parts of Virginia around Washington.
They would not allow, a mixed band to appear or --

West Virginia would -- wasn't particular about it, and some places in Virginia weren't too particular about it. It was according to what place you played. Some places they didn't -- they could care less. It's the proprietor of the places where you played. It wasn't always the law. It

was -- it wasn't always the cops or something like that. It was -- a lot of times it was the proprietor. I don't know whether he'd be frightened into doing this or what. You never know where the pressure was coming from. We didn't know anyway. But he could say that we can't do it, you know. It's not the policy here. So, you couldn't stand there and argue with him and find out is it against your policy or is it the law here or what. You never got that answer anyway, so it wasn't worth it to stand around and waste your time arguing about it anyway, you know.
(inaudible).
Because we all enjoyed playing and this was the whole scene. Huh?
Did Earl's band ever go South?

Oh, we played a lot of Southern dates but it wasn't no mixed band. Oh, yeah. Man, we lived in the South. The first time I met Illinois Jacquet and Clean Head and them, they were playing the Milton Larkins band in Houston, Texas. Yeah. This is early '30's. And they had a good band. Used to -- that was a good band that Milton had. They was blowing then, you know, way back there then. But I met those guys, I met Al Hibbler down in San Antonio, Texas. And then I also met Al in Little Rock, Arkansas. That's the --
That's where he's from -- isn't it?
Yeah, that's where I first met him. But

he used to travel all through the South. When I first met him was in Little Rock. Louis Jordan was from around in there too -- somewhere around in there. But it's just a hop, skip and jump down to Texas from Arkansas, you know.
How did you travel, by buses?
Buses. That's way --
(inaudible) -- his own bus?

No, no. We chartered a bus. There was a company in Newark that most all the bands chartered buses from. Newark Charter Company. I think the guy's name was Charlie something that had those buses. Yeah, that was before bands started working up the Greyhound Buses and buses of that sort. But it was something else.

But, I did -- I don't know. If you love music, nothing deters you, you know. That's how we felt. We just loved to play. And there were obstacles but if you were a true musician at heart, you wouldn't let them stop you. You'd just go on playing, man. Because we had a lot of fun playing. So, it made up for a lot of adversities, you know.
What about accomodations in the South?
Well, we usually would stay at somebody's home. And they had -- some of the big cities had a little

colored hotels in the South, but mostly rooming houses is where we would stay. Some people would just do that, put bands up and things of this sort, you know. And we knew a lot of these places because a lot of different bands would stop there, you know. And they would cook. A lot of these people at these homes, they would cook and you'd pay so much for a meal, you know, things. So, you didn't have no problem right there, you know.

Sometimes you had problems getting to the bathroom. They didn't have that many bathrooms all the times for a big band, but it always worked out. There was always a way. We made it, you know. But you have to love music really to go through that then, you know.

But the kids never had it so good as they have it, you know. We had to -- we were more like pioneers really back there then, just blazing away, you know, making the trail. Then we got so we'd know people in different cities, and we'd probably stay with them. We'd write, you know, before we came. That happened -- if you were working and worked in a popular band, you didn't have any problem because you knew somebody almost anywhere you went. You could stay with them, you know, friends or people of this ilk, you know. You had no problems.

He really enjoyed his band.
Oh well, that was his toy. He told everybody that was his plaything, that was his hobby, that was his toy. And it was.

Because he didn't have to go through all of that in years later, all those one-nighters and all that drudgery out there. He didn't have to do it but he loved it, he enjoyed it.
