No, Duke liked to navigate. He would-- you know he insisted (inaudible) Harry couldn't have made it if he wasn't telling Harry where to --

Yeah. He was beautiful though. He came up to where I'm playing in Honolulu about a year or so before he passed, you know. And he was talking to Sally, man, they were up there talking. He said -- you know, he had all the flowery words he used. And I play a few of his songs, "Mood Indigo", you know, and that knocked him out, and a few of
those things. He said I didn't know you could use a plunger. I says, oh, yeah. He's lots of fun though.
But music to him -- I don't know -- music to Duke was I think something that he couldn't have lived without. He had to -- he had to have it, you know, all the time. And he was always composing.
Right.

And Jimmy Jones used to tell me stories about Duke because Jimmy got very close to him in later years, you know. He says -- he says he never saw Duke when he wasn't either thinking of a tune or writing a tune or humming something. He says he never saw him when he wasn't in that frame of mind. And that's --
He'd have little scraps of paper. He'd jot things down -- in his pockets, and as soon as there was a portable piano invented, he had one in his hotel room, a little Wurlitzer.
Yeah.
He could screw the legs on, and he had it right beside the bed. And it'd be covered with little scraps of paper as well as manuscript paper.
Yeah.

He said he'd like wake up in the middle of the night, or in the middle of the day rather he slept, and think of a tune and do a few bars and go back to sometimes when sleep. And (unintelligible) he'd leave a place, he'd have a
whole bagful of fragments of things he was writing.

Well, you know, what they tell me. 'He never finished a lot of things that he started, a lot of tunes. And he told me himself that once he wrote a tune and they played it, he got tired of it then. He'd want to go on to something else, you know. Well, that's true genius, you know. He can't stay there. He's got to go on to something else. You know, interviewers used to ask him,
(unintelligible) Of all the tunes you've ever written, what's your favorite? He'd say, "The one I'm going to write tomorrow."
Yeah.
And he meant it.

He meant it. He's very sincere about that, yeah, because once he did the song, he was through with it then. He wanted to go on, and I don't blame him. He -- that's why he made so many different arrangements on the tunes that he had like because he'd get tired of it doing it that way. So, he'd just -- to make -- keep it interesting, he'd make another arrangement on it.
Uh-huh.

And you could see what he was doing. I could really see what he's doing all the time. He was creating another arrangement on top of that one, see. It's amazing how many versions of some of those tunes he recorded that he wrote different versions. He recorded them.
Uh-huh. He'd like arrange them for a different soloist or --
He did "Come Sunday" with Johnny Hodges, and the next time I heard him do it he had Ray Nance playing a violin solo, a beautiful violin solo on the thing.
Yeah, then he speeded up the tempo and Bunny Briggs tap danced it (inaudible) which was just "Come Sunday".
Yeah.
Faster tempo.
Do you ever see Bunny anywhere? I don't know what happened to him.
No. Last time was in New York, and that was quite a while ago.
Well, Duke really brought him out of the bag (unintelligible), you know, because --
Yeah.

-- nobody was hearing anything about him until Duke brought him doing these things. I regret that I never worked with Duke, and I had a chance to work with him once. But I -- when he wanted me I couldn't get away. I was tied up. I was tied up around New York at that time. I had some contractual things going. I couldn't get away from. And I told him that I really want to work with him though.
When was that that he wanted you?

This was during the time I was on 52nd Street. But I had signed several contracts. I had a contract then with Raymond Scott on those radio broadcasts he was doing, and I had one in the club. You know, like on 52nd street when you worked in a club, if you worked in a band like Tiny Grimes band, you really didn't work for Tiny, you worked for Chick Gorman, the guy who ran the club. And if he figured you had a little name, well, he would give you a little more money. You know, sometimes you'd be making more money than the leader. And he'd sign you to a little six month deal or something, but not too tied up.

I was just tied up enough not to be able to do that thing, you know. And then Norman Granz would come through, and I'd try to keep myself free that I could go on some of those things with Norman. I did do several -- about three of those tours with Norman.
Were they all in the United States or did you go (unintelligible)?
No, I never went to -- I never went anywhere but the United States and Canada with Norman. I never did make any of the European tours.
He wasn't going to Europe towards the beginning.
Not when I went him he wasn't.
It was later on (inaudible). of course, in he started taking things to Europe.

Uh-huh. Later on. And he really got -- he really got that thing going big in Europe though when he finally started it, you know. He got a big deal going in Europe. But he had a girl helping him who was a tremendous help, I thought. That was Martha Glaser.
Was she working with Norman?
She started out with Norman.
I didn't realize that.

And they kind of fell out because she took Erroll Garner off to tour and started managing him sort of. So, that was kind of the beginning of the end of that thing. But she was the one working with him. She was Norman's secretary back there then.
Oh.

When he first started those tours. And she was so sharp. She could look in a theater and tell you -- just look at it and tell him how he could scale it, and how much she could get from scaling the money, scaling it down. That's how sharp she was. She was -- I knew she was a sharp girl long ago. Yeah, Martha started out with Norman.
I didn't know (inaudible).
She was secretary. She was a big help to Norman back -- She's done a lot for Erroll
(unintelligible).
Yes, she has. You know, when we met

Norman, he was just running little jazz sessions out at the True Building. He's giving -- he'd give us (unintelligible) come into L.A. And he just finished UCLA, and when we'd come in L.A. he would try to run these sessions. And he'd give us $9.00 to go out there. And he had the money to play these little things out there at Trueville and little places like that. Willie Smith, Nat Cole, myself, Red Callender, we all used to go out and play them for him to help him out.
What -- do you remember what year that was?

Well, it'd have to be when I was with Lunceford, so that would be between '37 and -- it would be between '37 and '40 or '41. It had to be between there because that's -- those are the years I worked with Lunceford. And he was a good friend of Willie and (unintelligible) Fishelli, you know, because Norman didn't have a car then and Fishelli used to let him use their car. Sometime you talk to Fishelli about Norman. You'd learn.
Oh, I will.
It'd sure open up your eyes to a lot of things because -- we knew Norman when he had little patches on his britches and all around there. We knew him a long time ago.
Well, he doesn't dress too much better now. He just has (inaudible).
Yeah. He got the bread now, you know. He made a lot of money from the business.
Sure.

But I'll give him this. The guy was first class. Yeah, he was first class in doing things, you know. I liked him for that because he was the first -- one of the first guys I knew that really started paying the musicians some money when he made it, some fairly decent money, you know. And he travelled first class all the time. He lived in the best hotels, and everything was first class.

Now, he's a guy that fought that thing, that scene. He didn't like that scene and he fought it. I know he took us once, I think it was Lexington, Kentucky. And he told them if they didn't mix up that thing he wasn't going to play. Now, this is true. He did. I saw him do this. He did it.
What, the audience?
Yeah, and he did it in Norfolk, Virginia too. I saw him do it.
And he won?
Yeah, he won.
Really?

Well, he wouldn't have played if they hadn't done it and they knew he wouldn't. Well, the promoters must have been pretty heavy, you know, because you'd be surprised what money people can do in situations like this because

they control -- they control the politicians and people like that anyway, the money people like that. They give them X amount of dollars to help put them in office and they carry an awful lot of weight. These money men have changed a lot of things. Well, you'd be surprised that -- what that dollar has done. That dollar is -- you can't change a person's heart but you sure can change around those things going on out there.
Uh-huh.

No, you can't make the money or whatever, power -- (unintelligible)? It won't make a person's heart condition change. That's why there will always be problems. But you can really -- you can really change a lot of those stupid laws out there. You can (inaudible).
Duke used to say that the only basis for racial prejudice is economic.
Oh, he's true.
It's all a matter of money. It's --
It is.
Uh-huh.

It is because, you know, I'll tell you something I found. Everybody's prejudiced to a certain degree. Yeah, a lot of people I won't -- I don't want to be around regardless of what race they are. There's a whole lot of people I don't want to be around and they belong to a whole lot of different races, you know, some of the people. Really want

to look at it from that point of view. We all have certain prejudices but the bad thing is when you're prejudiced against a group of people per se. You know, that's when it's bad, because how can a whole race of people, any race of people, be bad. How can a whole race of people be good, by the same token. So, you know, so that's the only measuring stick that I use, you know, is try to -- a lot of people say it, say I judge a guy for what he is but they don't mean that. They don't believe that down in their hearts.

You talk to them long enough, you hear them make a statement. Then you say, oh, wait a minute. That's contradictory to what he's -- to the way he's acting, what he says and what he's doing, you know. You can read people like that and you can see it, you know. But there's always going to be a problem. There's always going to be some kind of problem.

The first thing is that people -- I don't think people have become educated enough to do away with problems because if they become educated enough, they'll educate the young ones enough to. You put a bunch of kids -- I've noticed this in Honolulu and a lot of places -- you put a bunch of kids of all nationalities together and they don't know nothing about all that stuff, man. They'll have a ball out there playing together. If you leave them alone you won't have no problem with them. But it's those older ones that teach them, well, listen, he's this and he's that. They don't -- they could

care less about that. They're just having fun playing. Because I look at it -- I look at it over in Honolulu, you know. All kind of kids, and they get out there and play and having a ball, man. They don't care nothing about nothing. That's why so many younger ones today don't have those hangups. They're not going to listen to some of the old ones who try to give them those hangups, and it's beautiful to see that they don't have them, you know.
Uh-huh. Yeah.

But music is always -- there's never been too many hangups among musicians. Even in the worst times, musicians have been pretty close together. Even way back in some of the worst -- under the worst conditions if they had to sneak around and do things together.

You know, I remember I went home to bury my mother in about -- around 1940, and Savannah, Georgia is a funny place. In '40 they weren't too open with things down there. But some of the -- my friends, the Caucasian friends I had down there knew I was coming and my mother had died -- musicians. Man, they had a flock of them around my house, you know, a whole bunch of them was around my house when I got there.

So, you know, down South when somebody's dead, you have a wake. You know, three or four days of drinking and food and everything there. So, there was a lot of liquor and everything in the house. And we were drinking. We were sitting on

the front porch, talking and shooting the breeze, smoking. And a policeman came by there and he called me. He says -- very nicely he says, he said, I know your mother just passed and I know you live in New York now. He says, I just thought I'd -- he says, we had a call, you know, that were a lot of mixing over here and everything like that. He says, and I know it's a solemn occasion. I had to come by to tell you this but, you know, some of the people in your neighborhood are afraid that something bad might happen because (unintelligible) bad might happen, you know, behind it.

So, he says, you know, I just advise you, you know, to let the -- I'm sorry. I don't like to bring this kind of message, but let the fellows -- tell the fellows they have to go home. So, I told them and, you know, I thanked him because he was real straight the way he came on with it. And the guys were really -- they were really drugged by the whole scene. But they had to go, you know.
But they could have sent a nasty one over there too, by the same token. You know, so they wasn't ready yet, you know. This was the '40's so, you know, I imagine it's a lot better now.
Yeah, I understand that amazing things are happening in Georgia.
Yeah, Atlanta anyway, I heard.
In Macon I heard --
Macon too, huh?
Yeah.

Well, that's good. It's good to hear those things that they're turning around, you know. Things are kind of turning around because with the musicians, they don't like -- they don't like those things happening like that, you know. Macou -- (unintelligible) where did James Brown come from, Augusta or Macon?
I'm not sure.
Yeah.
But I know a young civil rights attorney in Macon who --
Oh, yeah.
-- said he -- his mother lives in Los Angeles, and everytime he comes out here he has glowing stories about --
That's good.
-- the progress.
It's good to hear, you know.
(inaudible) is making.

That's real good to hear, yeah, because music has broken down a lot of barriers, you know. But guys really had to go through it, the older guys. They couldn't lose their cool. They had to really go through it to really help it, you know, because if they had blown up too much and
lost their cool, it would have set it right back where it was. But they had to go all the way through it.

I don't know. Most of the bands that I worked in though that when we did play the South, we found that we had real good friends on all sides, on both sides. Maybe a few -- a few less on one side or the other but we did have some real good. There was hope all the time because you saw some people who were really, they meant it. They were very sincere. They couldn't do but so much because their hands were tied. Usually it wasn't the people in the high positions who were like that.

But, you know, if enough of them feel like that, eventually it's going to build and be more and more until eventually something comes -- something good comes out of it, you know. I don't think we'd have made it if it wasn't for that type of person being around, you know. Before it was survival of the fittest, you know. A lot of them fell by the wayside. Oh, boy.
When was the first time you recorded?
The first time I recorded was with Earl Hines and that was in '33, about '33.
On what label?
I don't know but I got the album home. We did it in Chicago. Yeah, we did. I forgot what label it was but I got the album home.
Do you know if there's -- do you have a
discography or do you know that there is one that chronicles most of the things that you've done, that shows --
I don't have, no.
Have you ever seen one of like Earl Hines or Jimmy Lunceford's recordings that would show most of the things you're on?
Stanley Dance has got one I'm sure.
Now he's supposed to have put together a good one on Earl.
Yeah, he's got --
But does he also have Lunceford and --
I think he has because I'm working on a book and he told me he's got a lot of things to help me. He's going to kind of put it together for me, you know.
Oh.

So, he says I've got a lot of things, old pictures of you back there with Earl and everything, to put it together. He said I got more pictures than you'll ever dream of. So, I don't have them but he said he's got them, you know. I just got through talking to him about it. I'm going to do some tapes when I go back to Honolulu, you know.
Stanley and Helen were both at Dick Gibson's right?
Yeah, they were there, uh-huh. Have you ever been up there?
I never have.
You'd enjoy it.
I'm sure I would.
It's a lot of fun.
I've heard a lot of great things about it.

Well, it's a lot of -- it's different from probably any of those things you'll ever see. It's altogether different, you know. You're so close to the guys because, you know, it's one of those things. And, you know, you don't need no guards or nothing backstage or nothing. You know, everybody's just mingling, you know. And it's real close. And the guy who runs it is real good, you know. It comes off real good the way he does it. And there ain't no dull spots. It's going all the time and it's smooth, you know, the way it's going.

I like the way he does it. I like the way he treats people, you know. I'm not saying that the others don't treat them all right but the ones I've played, it's been a little too much protocol, you know. You can't walk backstage and see guys and things like this, and there ain't no backstage to walk here, you know. You're just in a spot and everybody's close together, you know.
It's a real party.
It is. It's just what he said. It's not

a festival. It's a party and it's fun. I really enjoy it. I really get a big bang out of doing it, you know. It's -- I think everybody that goes there feels the same way. It isn't like you're going to make a couple of bucks somewhere. You don't even think about it from that point of view. You just -- the guy just treats you so nice. And one thing I really enjoy about him is you'll always know what you're doing.

Some of them I've been on actually it's so -- they're so haphazard. Nobody ever doesn't seem to know what they're doing, when they're doing it or what. But this thing you know exactly what you're doing. Now, he might improvise and switch which is good, and switch things around a little bit. Sometimes he might say, oh, I think I'll put on four trombones and a rhythm section right here this time, and it works. He does it, you know. Say let's play a few numbers, two or three songs together before we bring the next group out. And it works. It's beautiful like that. Yeah, you know where you're at all the time.
And he shocked everybody when he brought out Faddis and -- Jon Faddis. Can you imagine that? And Eubie Blake. 22 and 94. He should name that number 2294.
Uh-huh.
Yeah, he should do it. It was fun. I'm going to let you go now.
Okay.
(Off the record)
Yesterday we were talking about Earl Hines and some of the members of the band (inaudible). I think we started to talk about Walter Fuller.

Yes, we did. And Walter was a very fine trumpet player with Earl and he was a good singer. He sang, you know, he had a jazz style of singing. And he tried to pattern somewhat after Louis, Louis Armstrong. But he had a high voice, a much higher voice than Lou. And he sang things with Earl, some of his popular things. "Rosetta" was one thing I remember in particular. It was a very popular record that Earl had out. And Walter Fuller sang the chorus on this. And it was a wonderful chorus that he did. In fact, they did a recreation of that -- Earl's particular record and they sent for me to come to -- from Honolulu to Decca -- Capitol Records did -- to come back to Hollywood. This was -- oh, this was probably about '67 or '68 -- and recreate Fuller's vocal chorus. I had to learn it all over again.

And I told them to get Fuller since Fuller was right in San Diego, but evidently they couldn't get in touch with him. And that's the way record companies do business anyway. But they had some fine -- other fine musicians in there too. There was Wally Bishop, the drummer, and I mentioned him previously. But he wound up in Europe. He's in Europe now. In fact, he was living in Amsterdam the last I heard about him,
and he was doing quite a bit of playing with different groups over in Europe. And whenever an artist came to Europe and he didn't bring his own band, well, he would back him over in Europe.

Also in the same band was a fine guitar player. He's passed away since. Lawrence Dixon was his name. And we had another fine trumpet player who doubled on alto saxophone, George Dixon. He was another fine man in that band. And, of course, there were three of us trombone players and I mentioned previously that two of these guys have passed away now. And that would be Billy Franklin and Louis Taylor.

And, of course, let me see. There was a bass player in there, Quinn Wilson. He did -- he was a good arranger. We call him Cupie. And he did quite a bit of writing for Earl back in those days. And he played a string bass and he also played a tuba. And he was a wonderful soloist on tuba, and Earl featured him quite a bit.

So, I don't know, that was a fast resume of the guys in the band with Earl. And, of course, as I mentioned previously that the guy I was more close to in that band was Ray Nance. And the reason I remember him so well was Ray was a fine musician and he had his own little group before he came with Earl. He had a fine little group and they were all youngsters playing around Chicago. And Ray always was a fine violinist. I think he played violin before he did trumpet.

But he admired Louis tremendously and, in fact, all of us did in those days. And so, he played trumpet on the style of Louis, and he sang a lot of Louis' things that Louis did. And he did a heck of a job because he could dance also, you know.

He was a terrific showman. And as most people found out when he went with Duke, he really got the proper exposure with Duke. And Duke admired him. Duke told us that Ray Nance never played a wrong note. You know, I thought that was a beautiful statement that he made about him.

Of course, I left Earl and I went to New York to join Jimmy Lunceford, and this is when I really began to get a little name among the public because Jimmy was very popular with recordings in those days. And we did a lot of -- had a chance to play a lot of solos. I was very fortunate because he didn't have a trombone player prior to the time I came in there that did a lot of solo work. So, I got an opportunity to play a lot of solos. He had two good trombone players but they weren't really soloists, you know. They were more just good section men. So, I got -- It was a good break for me going with him because I got most all of the solos to do.
Had you been soloing a lot with Earl Hines?
Quite a bit. Quite extensively. Of course, Earl would feature most of the guys in the band.
I know you mentioned getting calls --
long distance calls about your broadcasts, (Inaudible).

Yeah. That's right. I mentioned that. But one thing about Earl, he would let you grow in his band. He'd give you a chance to, you know, to develop. And this was hard to find in most bands because you had to have it when you got there. They didn't give you a chance to develop. And Earl gave all of us this opportunity. So, I think it was a stroke of good fortune for me going with Earl, and also the timing was good for me going with Jimmy Lunceford because as soon as I got in Lunceford's band, as I mentioned to you earlier, I got a chance to do some solos that really helped me tremendously because "Margie" was the first thing I did, as I told you earlier, that really helped me, you know. And it was a very popular recording, so --
That wasn't your first recording with Lunceford though, (Inaudible) was it?

No, I don't think "Margie" was my first. I don't -- I'm not sure, to be truthful with you. I know I recorded "Annie Laurie" with Lunceford around that time. I don't -- but I couldn't tell you right now exactly which was the first one. Like I was trying to recall the trombone player from Savannah to you that went to Spain and Europe. Now I know his name. His name was Herb Flemming.
Uh-huh.
It just came to me later. And -- but I

can't -- I really can't recall which record I did with Lunceford first but I know the most popular one I did with him was "Margie". And then I did a couple of songs with the -- later on with him, singing with the trio.
He had a vocal trio in there before I came and they had recorded "Blue Heaven", which was a popular recording. And they did this before I came in the band.
And that trio was who?

That trio was Sy Oliver, Eddie Tompkins, and Willie Smith. And when I came in the band he made a quartet. He added me onto the trio, and they did a couple of things that became very popular. One was "Ain't She Sweet" and the other was "Cheating on Me". And --
But it says the Jimmy Lunceford Quartet or the Lunceford Quartet vocals --
Uh-huh.
-- that's you, and Willie --

Sy Oliver and Eddie Tompkins. Yeah, see, when I -- they were the trio all the time before I went in the band. Of course, Dan Grissom was the vocalist. And out of us four guys I don't think any of us could really sing. But we had styles -- a little style going and it really helped. But Dan Grissom was really the true vocalist with the group, you know. And he had a -- he sang very high -- he had a high pitch voice back in those days. But he had -- he sang most of
the ballads and things of that sort. All we did was the jump tunes and things like that, you know.

Of course, Sy Oliver, as mentioned, Willie Smith and Eddie Tompkins, they weren't the only guys who sang tunes and myself, because Joe Thomas, the tenor man, he sang them, quite a few of the little rhythm things also.

So Lunceford had an abundance of guys doing things of this sort, and it was a good entertaining band, and this counted a lot, you know, with people, because visually they were good, and the band played good, you know.
How about the DandRidge sisters?

They were with us, and they did a couple of recordings with us, and I can't remember the year, but I know it was in the late '30's or the early '40's, and they -- we did some theater tours, and they looked good on the stage, you know, and Dorothy and her sister Vivian, and the with them other girl was not a sister. Her name was Etta Jones. And she later married Gerald Wilson. This was Gerald's first wife -- the arranger on the West Coast.
And they had a good -- they had a very good visual trio, you know. They were competent singers. I don't think

they were great singers, but they were competent, and they looked good; they were young, and they were nice looking girls, and they dressed well, and they looked nice. And they made quite a few tours with us, theater tours they did mostly, and we backed several big stars when I was with that band.

One of the stars we backed was Bill Robinson, Bojangles. We did about 20 -- about 22 weeks of theaters with Bill Robinson, and our main thing was to back him, and he -- he had a pianist who traveled with him, Putney Dandridge and, of course, we -- there were certain recordings that we did that he liked, and he liked to tap dance to these things. One of them was Ain't She Sweet. And we used to sing that and play it softly, very softly, and he would come out and tap dance to it, and he liked -- For Pancers Only. We used to do that for him.

But we played it very soft, because he was a great artist, I thought, you know. I always used to watch this man perform, and he really had something going there. He could really reach the people. We played lots of theaters with him all through the Middle West, through Texas. There was a chain of theaters through Texas -- I think Majestic Theaters, I think, was the name; I'm not sure of that chain -- and we played quite a few theaters throughout the country. We did 22 straight weeks of theaters with him, Lunceford's band and --
What other stars did you work with with Lunceford?

Well, he would -- he would have been the most prominent star that we worked for, but we used to -- we used to always back choruses, girls, chorus girls, and this would be at the Apollo Theater and theaters of this sort. And now, we would play the music for quite a few of their acts, like Buck & Bubbles and acts of this sort back there then, John Bubbles and Buck Washington, his partner.

So we played for quite a few acts, and they were fine back there acts, then in -- I can't even recall the name of all the acts, but some of them were outstanding in my mind, for instance, as the two I named, you know.
How many shows a day would you play in a theater?

Well, about four shows a day, we did, uh-huh. And they would run a movie, a short movie between them shows, but actually the first show would go on, oh, I -- and this is, approximately speaking, around 12:00 noon or somewhere, and the last show would go on about 11:00 at night, and this was the way those -- yeah, this was the way those theaters operated.

Of course, some days we'd do more shows. On the weekends probably we'd do five shows sometimes. And then once a week they'd a midnight show at the -- at the Apollo Theater, so this was a long show. We'd just go on until time without end on that show, and a lot of performers would come in to watch that show, you know.
Approximately How long engagements did you get? I mean a week, two weeks? How long
did you stay in a theater?
One week, never over a week. No, we never -- we never stayed over a week. No, it was just the one week engagement.
Was that seven days?

Seven days, yeah. Yeah, we never stay -- we never stayed over -- we played a week, and that was it. And, of course, the biggest portion of our work was one nighters back in those days, you know. Well, we relished the thought of doing theaters. You know, even if you were tied up all day, at least you were in one place, you know. You weren't jumping all around.
