You know, he had a big heart, because he came to Honolulu later on, and he called me up to his room, you know, after work. I was working over there at the same hotel he was living in, at the Ilikai at that particular time.

And so I went up to his room, and we had a long talk. He says, I can see your point. Now, I see; I didn't know you had those problems with your wife being sick like that. He said, well, I can see your point now.
You know, everybody seems to have warm things to say about Louis.
Oh, well, he was a warm person. Let's face it, you know. I don't see how you could help but saying warm things about Louis. He was Mr. Warmth, we'll call him.
And generosity too.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
What I've heard -- always looking to help somebody.

Yeah, but he didn't want that out, you know. He didn't want the press or nobody to know about those things, when he helped somebody, because he really didn't do it for publicity. Like a lot of people do, you know, and they want to give you something on TV or something.
(Laughter)
Big show, you know.
Then you mentioned also the fact that -- after rehearsal that when -- one of the times Louis came to Honolulu, he had Tyree Glenn with him on trombone, and he asked you to show Tyree a good time.

He kept me up all night. Louis didn't like to sleep, for one thing. I tell you something about Louis. Louis and Duke had similar qualities. They always want people around them. And Louis didn't -- he didn't like to sleep, so he called me up, and he had me with him all night to show Tyree Glenn how he should be singing some of those things, 'Old Rockin'Chair' and some of the things that I used to do with him.
I didn't do this originally with him. Jack Teagarden did them, 'Rockin' Chair', who was, incidentally, was a very

fine, a great musician. He did 'Rockin' Chair' originally with Louis, and Louis always wanted somebody to sing, you know, sing things with him, because he had Velma over there as a foil, you know, and she -- they were fantastic team together. Velma wasn't a great singer or nothing like that, but she certainly was the right foil for Louis. I would have hated to have followed them on stage, man.

But Louis kept me up all night, up until about 9:00 o'clock in the morning, showing Tyree how to do these spots with him that -- because how I really got to doing well was Louis helped me, you know. He'd say, now, when I get -- when I mug like this, you do that or you do this, and over the long period of time I worked with him, I picked up a lot of those little mannerisms to do with working with him.

And so he wanted me to show Tyree, and I showed Tyree. I was helping Tyree on a lot of those things. See, Louis -- anybody could have learned from Louis. I had a long discussion with John Hendricks one time. We went up to Monterey, and I don't know if you remember this particular year, and Dave Brubeck and his wife had written a thing called 'The Real Ambassadors.' In fact, it's out on a record.

And we had a long discussion after rehearsal, John Hendricks and myself. He said, you know, I kind of envy you. He said, man, you're sitting there working under the greatest teacher that you can find. I say, I know it. He's speaking

about Louis, because you could learn an awful lot from Louis if you were observing, if you were aware. Anybody could, not me, just me, but anybody else. The guy knew -- he knew phrasing; he knew timing. He was a master of timing and phrasing and little innuendoes that he would put into things, you know, like I was trying to help Teddy with some of those things at rehearsal today.

He knew them. And stand him aside, you know, if you're really observant, some of it would rub off on you, you know, and I got a lot of -- I thought I knew something about the stage and all. I knew nothing. When I got with Louis, I found out I knew nothing about the stage. He was a master of that stage. You had a hard time following Louis on that stage. I don't care who you were.

I tell you something that happened when I was with Louis. We had a tour with Benny Goodman and Benny Goodman's big band, and so Benny had some money put up in the tour. Joe Glaser's office was booking it. And so they decided to put -- Benny decided to put Louis on first. You know, that old show business thing. I'll get the last shot at you.
So he did. And when he put Louis on first, he could hardly get on afterwards.
(Laughter)
He had a hard time getting on. So after about a week of that, he -- John Hammond was out there on the road, watching it
going on, and he said, let's put Louis on last. So they did. And I don't know why he ever did that. So the -- when Benny went on, people would be out in the lobby smoking, waiting for Louis.
(Laughter)

And Benny got so mad one night, he took his glass and -- he had some scotch and soda. He threw it against the wall. So he told -- he told them, he said, hey, that guy ain't doing nothing but clowning out there. He was talking about him and Velma, said, that's not music, you know, clowning.

Well, you see, what he forgets is Louis wasn't only a great musician. Louis was a great showman on top of it. So there isn't nothing wrong with using showmanship out there along with your music, a combination, and this is what Louis had. This is one of the things that made him so great.

He could play one of the greatest choruses you ever heard in your life, and after he got through, he could give some little mannerisms that was greater than the chorus, you know. So he'd shoot you down one way or the other.

And these are things that he naturally had. Nobody taught him that. He didn't learn that from anybody. Those were -- it was just Louis. He was just Louis. It's just like Duke, you know, and the smile that he would have out there and his talk. Nobody could teach Duke anything about speaking. It was him, because it wouldn't sound right, that same thing

he said coming from somebody else. If he wrote it and gave it to the average guy to say, it just wouldn't sound right. That was Duke. That was him. That's how he felt inside. Well, this is the way Louis was, how he expressed himself, and these are many of the things that I learned from Louis and a lot of other guys there in front of -- because, let's face it, all the greatest singers, jazz singers all learned from him.

Billie Holiday said all she listened to was Louis and Bessie Smith and people like that. Sinatra said he listened to him and Billie Holiday. And Bing said he listened to Louis and he -- who else, man, is there, you know?
Do you know of any specific ways of the playing or the singing you changed from having been associated with Louis? What were --

I don't know. I would say I learned a lot about timing from Louis. I learned a lot about building, like not starting out too strong, just building things and, you know, starting easy and building things up. And these things are important.

But timing, I think the greatest thing I accomplished from Louis was not trying to put everything into -- right away into something, not trying to do all the things I knew right away into a chorus, but taking it easy and building the thing up to a climax, you know. And he was a master at that. But
some guys you hear, they start out like a house a-fire. Then they kind of calm down. But that wasn't his way of doing things. He started out easy, and he would build. He had a climax going.

I learned that from him. I -- I certainly learned stage presentation from him, because I learned how to handle myself on the stage, you know, for -- to relax more on the stage, not get out there and jump up and down like a bouncing ball or something and beat my brains out. You know, some guys go --
Did you ever do that?
Huh?
Did you ever do that?
No, but I learned not to do it, to be much more relaxed; like some people, when they get out there, they're jumping up and down so much, they can't hold their horn straight and play right, you know.
And Louis always did seem --
He was relaxed.
He knew relaxation, right.

He was relaxed, and this guy was -- he had the whole thing, really. Believe me, he had the whole thing going there. He was -- he was complete. And he knew the stage;like, for instance, we'd start playing a thing some nights, and he wouldn't -- he wouldn't like the way the

way the response was, and right away he'd change and go into something. He wouldn't do the regular thing, you know. He'd go into something else. He'd handle them, you know. He knew how to -- he knew people. He could -- he could read an audience. And this is hard to do. It's very hard to do.

I've seen some top musicians that -- Benny couldn't do it. I've seen some very fine, excellent musicians that couldn't read that audience. They would -- they would give the wrong program. It was good, but they played -- you could find no fault with it. It would be flawless almost, but it would be the wrong presentation for that particular audience.

This is what he knew. Nobody could teach you that. These are things you try to watch and pick out, and I guess it took him years to become, to get to that point where he could really do that. But I watched him. I watched him like a hawk.

And John Hendricks told me he used to watch him just as hard. You know, John knows -- he knows what he's doing. He's no dummy, man. He said he watched -- he watched Louie, and he learned an awful lot from Louie. Anyone could. Duke loved him. You know, did you hear the record, thing we did with Duke, Louis' little band and Duke at the piano?
Yes. Yes, I did.
It was a cute little thing they did. It was very cute. I enjoyed it. I really enjoyed doing that
thing, and we did Duke's tunes, you know, on those things, and it was cute.
Now, Duke's what -- four favorite -- Louis, Sidney Bechet, Django Reinhardt and Willie the Lion, I think.
I think Willie the Lion was one.
These four people were inspirations?

Yeah, well, you had to like Sidney. If you know Sidney -- if you know Sidney, man, his playing, you had to like Sidney, because he was daring, you know. He just -- he's strong and daring. He took charge, you know, when he was playing, and he loved to play. He was a reckless player. He just went on in there, you know, and you had to like him. Anybody --
Did you work with him?

No, I never did have -- I jammed with him one night, as I told you, in Paris when we went over there and did the Edward R. Murrow thing, but I never had the pleasure of working with him. I've worked right across the street from him on 52nd Street for a long time, when he was at Jimmy Ryan's, you know.

No, he was a fantastic player and a fantastic person. It's funny, though. He never got proper recognition until he went to France over there, and they really took to him over there. He didn't come back, once he got over there.
(Laughter)
They really took to him. I understand they have a statue in a park over there of him, you know, not in Paris, Antibes -- someplace an- -- something.
Antibes?
Yeah, somewhere around in there. I've never been there, but that's where they're supposed to have a statue of Sidney over there. Oh, yeah, he deserved it. He deserved it, you know. He really did.
How about traveling with Louis Armstrong? That was much later in comparison with the big band travel we were talking about before, but Louis always went first class.

He did, but it was hard. I'll tell you something about one-nighters. I don't care how you do them, they're hard. But at least it was first class, the way we traveled with Louis. It was -- it was rough, but it was first class.
You had nights off sometimes, didn't you? It seems to me I used to see the --

When I first went with Louis, we didn't have many nights off because he was strong then, you know, and he was very strong. And he played hard, and he didn't want to relax. But later on as he got a little weaker, then we started having nights off. See, Louis had a case history of a
bad heart for a long time.
For how long?

Well, at least 20 years. Yeah. I know we did a thing over in Spoleto, Italy, you know, and he had a pretty bad heart attack over there. He had to take off. We did an Ed Sullivan thing over there. And he had to take off. That Carlos Menotti thing, you know, he did over there one year, and he had to -- he had to take off for about two, three weeks, and what -- he came back soon as it was, about three weeks after a heart attack like that.

They -- Ed Sullivan was crying. He didn't think he would make it. But Louis was strong. Louis was perhaps the strongest guy I ever worked around, because he -- he didn't -- you know, he didn't try to live carefully or anything like this. He lived the way he wanted to live, and the heck with it. That's how he lived, you know?
Didn't you say he also had something -- problem with coughing or congestion or --

His -- he had a bad congestion problem. He used to cough hard all the -- for years, years and years. He coughed hard all the time. But he used to do some of the damndest things. He'd eat a big meal over there in Italy, and he'd get on a great big fan and go get in a chair and lay back and go to sleep, and I used to look and wonder how he'd do things.
So his doctor traveled with him. Dr. Sheff told us,
don't try to emulate this guy, you know, because you'd die probably tomorrow, he said. He took a laxative every night for 40 years.
Swiss Kriss, right?

Every -- before Swiss Kriss he took Pluto Water, and it came in a bottle. It's strong stuff, you know. And then he got on his herbal Swiss Kriss. Later -- I think the reason Glaser helped switch him to that Swiss Kriss was it comes in little packages, and it's herbal and it's easy to carry. With that -- you know, traveling by plane all the time, carrying cases of that Pluto Water, I think Glaser was watching that bill go up --
(Laughter)
-- on the plane rides. So he switched him over to that, yeah.

Well, I remember seeing Louis' itinerary the same time I looked at Duke's itinerary and (inaudible) out of ABC (inaudible). Louis has always looked a little more considerate, like somebody who cared about his health and his strength, that there would be a day off once in a while, and there wouldn't be as long jumps to do. Duke used to have the most absurd itinerary. He'd go 1,000 miles, and then he'd back up 500, and then he'd go 1,000 again.
We used to do it. But when Louis started getting sick, then he started lightening up on them. We used to do the same thing.
And then Duke used to say, Joe Glaser doesn't care as much about me as he does Louis. He gives Louis better dates.

Well, I don't think Joe Glaser cared as much about his own mother as he did Louis, if you really want to know the truth, because -- did you ever know that story of how Glaser got to be Louis' manager?

Barney said something about them both coming -- on a boat coming back from England, Louis' manager at that time wanted to teach Louis a lesson and said, I'm going to sell your contract, and Joe was there or something. Was that what happened?
No.
What happened?
Louis told me the story himself. Louis had a manager by the name of Collins, and from what I can gather, he was a big crook, you know.
I've heard that.

And they were going to Europe, and Collins got drunk. John Hammond was on the same boat. And Collins got kind of drunk, and he called Louis a black nigger. And Hammond heard it and knocked him down. And Hammond was a young guy then. Louis told me this story. And he told Hammond -- when he told -- he told Collins, he said, I'm through with you;when we get over this trip, I don't want no
more to do with you. So that's why he had a lot of managerial trouble when he was over in Europe, and he fired Collins and got rid of him.

But Collins had a contract on him. So Louis remembered that he had worked for Joe Glaser, and Joe Glaser was tied in with some pretty rough boys around Chicago. So Louis, when he came back, he got in touch with Joe, and he told Joe, he said, I'm having a lot of trouble with this guy managing me, said, I'm kind of scared. He said, I don't know what he's going to try to do to me.

He says, but I want you for my manager. So Glaser said, you got to be crazy. I don't have no lot of money to handle your manager. Glaser didn't have nothing, and he used to have the Sunset Cafe, but, you know, that was owned by the boys, you know, in Chicago.

So finally Louis talked him into being his -- they never did have a contract. They shook hands. For 45 years he was his manager, only on a handshake. And Glaser, on the strength of being with Louis, Louis used to tell us stories about it. They used to ride the bus down South with Glaser, and Glaser didn't -- none of them hardly had enough to eat with, and he says, but on the strength of that, Louis started getting real popular. Glaser started getting good P.R. for Louis.
And on the strength of that, Glaser built that big

office and everything up there just on the strength of Louis. So Glazer used to tell everybody, he said, look, I might give anybody a screwing, but not him. See, he's my man. He put me where I am today.

And Louis said Glazer wanted to give him a big interest in that office. He said, man, I don't want no business. He said, you just take care of my money for me. He said, I don't want no business. And so everybody figured that Glazer was giving Louis a raw screwing with that money and all, because Louis -- money didn't mean -- never did mean nothing to Louis.

He'd have about ten grand in his pocket and four, five days later he had nothing. He'd go back, hey, Joe, give me ten more. Joe would give it to him. And this is how he went all the time. Well, all the meantime Glazer was holding the money for him, but nobody believed it. Who the hell would believe that a guy like Glazer was holding money?

But Glazer told everybody. He said, 'listen, I'll give everybody a screwing, but not him.' And so finally when deal with down and Lucille had about eight, nine, ten million dollars, you know, and they could see what the whole deal was, that Glazer was -- was up to his word, you know, but he figured he didn't have to prove that to nobody. He knew he was keeping money for Louis, you know, and he did.
He didn't have to take -- why did he have to take it?
He's giving everybody else a royal -- what you call 'em, you know -- so it made no difference what they thought of him. He knew how he and Louis stood.
And I always said I didn't believe either one of them could live without the other. One of them died, the other one wouldn't last much longer, and that was the case.
(Inaudible).

Well, Glaser died, and Louis didn't last much longer than that. That's how close they were. They were much closer than anybody ever realized. But we knew it in the -- we knew how close, and he worried like hell about Louis. He heard Louis had a cough over in Europe, he'd be on the next plane over there or something. That's how tight they were.

And Joe Glaser, the way he'd talk, you figure he didn't care about Louis or nobody else, but he did. He cared about Louis. So, you know, the guy's the one who put him in business, put him up where he was. He could never done that without Louis.
(Inaudible).

Yeah. Well, I was -- in a way I was glad that he got hold of Duke because I know Duke would never want for no work, making big money with him, you know, and Duke was never going to stop playing. You could see that.
Oh, absolutely not.
And I don't think William Morris could have gotten a lot of lucrative deals for Duke that Joe and them did.
No, he kept, he absolutely kept him working.

Well, it was a different scene with him and Duke and him and Louis. You can understand why he cared more for Louis than he did anybody. But everybody around that office knew that. They knew that Joe cared more for Louis than he did for his own family. He wasn't very close to his family in Chicago, but he was very close to Louis.

He was worried about Louis' wives. He didn't want him to marry this one and that one. He was always worrying about everything, you know. He knew every move Louis made. Louis would tell him. He would call him up and tell him. See, Louis would let him know anything that went wrong. He had Joe's private number. He'd call him up any hour of the night or anything and tell him.

And they had a close thing going together, you know. And both of them are around the same age. But I saw a lot of things that with Louis and that I would have probably never seen. Some of the things I saw with Louis was how close -- how much -- a big statesmen and everything, how they felt toward Louis, you know, that they loved Louis. I'm talking about top people in the world, you know, how they clamored around him, and they asked him for advice. And here's a guy
went to second or third grade, man. He's telling Tshombe down there, see, Daddy, you ain't doing right, you know, one day in front of brought them all out the -
Did he say that?

You got to -- you taking all that money; you ain't giving out none. Man, you ought to take some and leave some. That's how he'd talk, you know, and he's talking to Tshombe, and that's how he talked to him, you know. And sure enough, he was right. You know, we didn't realize it. But we knew Louis was staying with Tshombe, so we knew he must have known something, because he stayed at Tshombe's house.

And we were worried about that because Tshombe had a big problem with Lumumba back in those days, you know, and we all felt like Lumumba was right, which now I'm sure we had the right idea, and Tshombe was going along with big business, which proved itself to be true later on.

But we were afraid that Louis was going to get poisoned or something because Tshombe had a lot of servants and all, you know, around there, and being in that house, you know, anything could happen, you know. But he seemed to have had a charm with him.

Louis was -- I ever tell you about some of the interviews Louis had over there in -- oh, man, we played with -- we went to Beirut with Louis. So these guys who booked us down in Beirut, these two brothers, George and -- I forget

their last name. Well, man, these guys were high all the time. They'd be smoking that hashish, so he's smoking it along with them. So they told us one day, how come you guys going to Israel? So he says, told me, ask Louis. So, you know, so then they cornered Louis, got him, some newspaper guys there one night and -- down in the basement dressing room, and said, about four, five newsmen say, says, told Louis, "say, how come you going playing for them damn Jews down in Israel?"
So Louis sort of looked at them, and he said, "let me tell you something. When I go down there, the first thing they going tell me, how come you play for them damn Arabs over there?"
(Laughter)

That was -- that's the interview now with these press guys. Man, he told them. He says, "let me tell you something, man. That horn, you see that horn? That horn ain't prejudiced." He said, "a note's a note in any language." (Inaudible) on the floor down in the back. We was laughing, man.
Me and Billy Kyle were falling

So, sure enough, when we got down there, that's the first thing those guys told Louis; so Louis told them, he said, I told them that you guys are going to say the same damn thing. So ain't none of you no better than the other one. You's as bad as they are, man. And so he told the press all that.
(Laughter)
And, sure enough, that's what had happened.

We went from there to Cairo, Egypt, and when we were down in Cairo, they all gathered around Louis and asked him was he for the Zionists, say, are you for the Zionist cause? He said, what is that, Daddy? So they told him, said, you helped the Jews a lot. He said, yeah, I help them. I help anybody. I help you. You need help? I help anybody, he said.

So he told them. He said, let me tell you something. This is the way he talked. They're all about 24 newspaper reporters. Said, let me tell you something right now. Don't you forget that, hear, he said. So this is the way he talked. He says, I'm going to tell you this. I got a trumpet, and I got a young wife, and I ain't got time to fool with none of the stuff you guys talking about, and he walked off and left them all in the lobby, man. He went up to his hotel room.
Oh, I could tell you some stories about this guy, man. He was funny. He was really funny. He had -- Ernie Anderson was -- you know Ernie Anderson?
No.

Well, Ernie Anderson used to be the PR man for -- he loved Louis all his life. In fact, he's the guy set up Nixkin the Village and all those -- Eddie Condons and all, because he loved jazz. But he's a brainy guy. He lives in London, and he's PR man. So Ernie hung around us all the time. And Ernie, when we made big tunes, Joe Glazer would
stand there, and I guess they paid him big money to go with us, and Ernie -- and Louis was real tight.

And Ernie and I got to be real good friends, because I got to run around with him a lot when he was out traveling with us when Louis was busy or something. But Ernie was PR man for John Huston for years and years. John Huston didn't go nowhere without Ernie. And now he's PR man for Charles Bronson. And he came over to Honolulu not long ago. But me and Ernie were talking once about -- and Ernie took him -- I said, Ernie, what did he say? Ernie took him to an interview with the Pope.

I said, Ernie, tell me, what the hell happened up there, you know? So I knew there had to be a story there. So Ernie said, well, the Pope, let me tell you, Trummy, he said, you won't believe this. He said, the Pope asked him was he married. And so he told him, yeah, Daddy, I've been married five times.

He told him, you got any children? He said, no, Daddy, but I'm working at it every night. He say he cracked up, the Pope. He said he couldn't ask him no more. He couldn't say no more. And he was telling me this story, but I know that sounds like Louis. You know, his valet worked for him for years, Doc Pugh -- we call him Doc Pugh because he used to buy all of Louis' vitamins for him.
Louis, man, he'd take vitamins. He'd say, give me

two red ones, three green ones. He took them by the boatload. So anyway, Doc Pugh passed away, and this was after I left the band and guys were telling me this story. So Artie Shaw walked in the dressing room one night, and he missed him and said, hey, Louis, where's Doc Pugh. He said, man, Doc Pugh is dead. He said, what was wrong with him? Louis looked at him and said, man, you crazy; when you dead, everything is wrong with you, you know.
(Laughter)
But who would think of that answer but Louis? And these are, you know, you could --
(Inaudible) --

-- you could go on all night telling stories about this guy, and that's the kind of guy he was, man. One guy said, hey, Louis, how's everything going? He said, hey, Daddy, white folks still in the lead. He kept on walking.
(Laughter)

He just -- came off the top of his head, these things. He was funny. He was -- I mean in the dressing room he was like that. Out on the street he -- just that was his way. He didn't work at it. It was just there, man. It was -- he was a funny man. He kept me in stitches all -- all the time. You couldn't feel down around him because he always had something funny to say, you know. And that -- he meant it
-- he told me one day -- I never forgot this. He said -- it was in Paris, and some people had just took us down to Louvre, you know, to see all --

So he told me when he came out, he said, Trummy, you see all them pictures with the eyes and all coming out? He talking about modernistic paintings, you know. He said, did you see all those things? I said yeah. He said, what did you notice about them? I said, well, it's real modern, Louis, you know. He said, let me tell you something. You know who put those things up? I said no. He said, the Russians put them things out to confuse the Americans.

He said, if you see a horse, you know that's a horse, don't you? If you see a rose, you know -- I couldn't believe it, what he was talking. I told Billy Kyle Collins, and he laid on the floor laughing. I couldn't believe it. This guy -- laughed about two weeks until my stomach hurt me. I didn't know whether he was putting me on or whether he really, really believed it, but I couldn't believe it. I just couldn't -- these things -- he used to come on right out of the clear sky with, things like you just couldn't believe.

I couldn't believe things that he used to tell me, like funny, man. But, yeah, we go in Europe, and here's Princess Margaret and all of them like that, asking him about -- questions about things, and he's sitting up there having court with these big people.
(Laughter)

And I used to look at him. We went to Japan, and you know, we played a little thing at an American club over there, and this night the Prince -- Akihito and his wife were there, and he wound up out there dancing with them, and you just don't do that with the Prince's wife, with the Princess. And this is against all protocol, but everybody was just laughing and dying laughing.

The next day he had got with some newspaper reporters. He was drinking, so they had him pull off his shirt, you know, and he had a little round belly. So they took it -- he's sitting on the floor, and they took his picture, and they had a big sign, a thing on the newspaper, black Buddha, you know.
(Laughter)

And Louis, the funniest thing, he's grinning, and his belly, little belly out there, and he just was a funny cat. And this thing went to all, Associated Press, all over, United -- when he did something like that, it just made headlines.

We went down to South America, and the people were grabbing at him, and they'd get his handkerchief and take a cigarette out of his mouth and everything, just want to touch him. He went and bought a baseball catcher's mitt, and he put it on. He came out to the airport. He had the guy go in town and get him because so many people was waiting, and
he came out to the airport with this catcher's mitt. So the guy, he says, ain't going to let them ruin my chops, man.
(Laughter)
I could tell you stories just about Louis all night, just about sit here all night, but this is how the guy was.
you were doing something with
You mentioned (inaudible). I don't think I know about that.

We were doing the Ed Sullivan show then. It was for the Ed Sullivan TV show. And it was during that week that they had that, all that going on over there, and what the heck is the singer's name? One of the opera singers, she's kind of hefty girl. She sang "Sunny Side of the Street" with us. I can't think of her name. But she was on that Sullivan show.
Probably her name will come to me later, but I don't -- you're losing me right now.
Helen Traubel?
No, no. That wasn't it. She lives up around New England. I can't think of it now.
Maybe it'll come to you later.
Yeah. But Louis did many things through Europe, you know, and --
Chilton, it mentioned you were working with Claude Hopkins.
According to (inaudible)
I did. I worked up at the Hurricane Club there with Claude Hopkins. And who else?
Paul Baron's CBS Orchestra. (inaudible)

Yeah. Well, I played with Paul Baron, because Paul used to do the Mildred Bailey show, and on that show she used a lot of jazz musicians on that show. Teddy Wilson used to play it. Charlie Shavers played it; Stuff Smith played quite a few of those shows, and sometimes Mary Lou Williams would sit in on some of those shows.

Yeah, we did it regularly. I was a regular on that show, and so was Charlie, and so was Teddy.
network was Was it? (inaudible)?
I don't know. It was radio. I don't know whether it was CBS or -- it was -- I don't know, but it was the Mildred Bailey Show. I remembered that, yeah. And I also played with Raymond Scott.
I think you mentioned that. (inaudible)
Yeah, I think he was CBS. I'm not sure, but Charlie was on that band too, Charlie Shavers and myself. We were on that band together.
How long were you there?
With Mildred Bailey? I don't know. I guess I did about one season of those shows, you know. About 12 or 13 weeks, something like that.
with Claude Hopkins that - (inaudible) was that just the one engagement?
Just one engagement. I played up there

with Claude for about two months, something like that. Joe Garland was on the band, saxophone player I mentioned that wrote In the Mood and Leap Frog and some of those things. He was on the band. Rudy Powell was on the band. He changed his name to Sid Achim or something. I don't know what name he -- but he was on the band as Rudy Powell, saxophone player.

Trying to see if I remember any of the other guys. I know there was two of us trombones was Ted Kelly. He was a drummer. I don't know if you remember him. He didn't get to be too big a name. I don't remember too many of the guys because I didn't stay there long, you know, just about a couple months. Yeah, I played with Claude up there.
You -- did you work for Norman Granz for two years, in '46 and '47, before you left or was that just --

Just tours -- just parts of those two years, the spots -- a tour wouldn't last over eight or ten weeks, you know, so I made two tours with him really, two tours would sound better than two years, because Norman never kept anything going for two years. Only attractions he ever had was Ella and Oscar Peterson, those -- he worked them steady, but he didn't keep anything with them.
Of course, Ella always used a trio, as I know of. Tommy Flanagan's been playing for her now about 17 years, her little group.
And Johnny Bothwell in January (inaudible) in 1945?

Bothwell? Well, Bothwell and I were actually with Boyd Raeburn together. We were in Boyd Raeburn's band together. So was Serge Chaloff and -- who else? Little Benny, Benny Harris, a little trumpet player. Benny was on that band, and Diz played a little while with Boyd Raeburn.
You recorded, didn't you?
With who?
Did you record with them? (inaudible)? Or you didn't record with Boyd Raeburn?

No. I didn't record with Raeburn. No, I didn't -- I didn't record with Raeburn. I played a few jobs with him, though, you know. He had a piano player that wrote real good. His name was John Handy -- George Handy.
Oh, yes.
George Handy. George was an arranger on that band. He wrote real good. I remember him back there. He wrote some of those things like 'Boyd meets Stravinsky' and some of those far out things.

I keep asking that question. Oh, this is why (inaudible). I knew there was a reason. My -- according to my notes here, Barry Ulanov said, and in his book that the Sir Charles, Raeburn's band in 1945 recorded with Dizzy, Benny Harris, (inaudible), Oscar Pettiford and four sides (inaudible) featuring Trummy Young.
Huh. I might have done something with
him. I don't know. I can't recall. I know Dizzy and I played on the band together, Serge Chaloff, Benny Harris.
Was he there when you were?
(Inaudible)
Pettiford?
Pettiford was with Barnet with me. I don't know if -- Pettiford might have been on that band. I can't -- I don't recall no Pettiford being with Raeburn. He might have been.
Mert Oliver mentioned you once, and --
Mert was a bass player on the band.
Yeah, I remember --
(Inaudible). In '45 --
And Candy was -- Don Lamond -- he's got Don Lamond on? Yeah. Earl Swope was another trombone player on that band.
Yeah, in '40 --
Ollie Wilson, is his name on there?
They didn't list the complete personnel --
(Inaudible) just mentioned some of them.
But Bothwell was on that band, Johnny Bothwell.
But that was the only time you worked with Bothwell?
That's the only time, yeah. Bothwell did get a band together later, but I didn't play with him.
Benny Goodman, February to August, 1945?
Yeah, I worked a few months with Benny, and the time I was with him, Slam Stewart was with him, and Red Norvo was with him same time I was with him. Who else was with him? He had a big band.
What did you do - tour one-nighters or what?

Yeah, we did one-nighters, couple theaters, mostly one nighters. I didn't work long with him, though. I played down at Atlantic City with him for about a week at that Steel Pier down there. Yeah, I played down there. And Jane Arby was singing with him then, and I saw her not long ago. She's married to a producer or something like that out in Hollywood here, uh-huh.
And then Tiny Grimes, it has listed, both 1944 and 1946, (inaudible)?
I worked with him two times, yeah. I told you once we backed Billie Holiday down there. I played with him a couple of times.
And in Honolulu when you stayed -- where did you go to -- who were you working with when you went there with C. P. Johnson?
We worked at one club there called the Hula Rhumba. Is that mentioned there?
No, it isn't. I just wondered and then - name --
But mostly we played the different
islands, just gave concerts on different islands. And then it said you —
(inaudible) when you stayed there, you worked with Art trio.
I did, yeah, little trio from San Francisco in the Brown Derby over there, club called the Brown Derby. Was a real junk club, what you call it, the Brown Derby, I guess, for lack of a better name.
What did Art (inaudible) play?
He played bad bass.
(Laughter)
And he went back to San Francisco, and he got into real estate and made a fortune. Yeah. He didn't play very well.
And then you also led your own group.
Yeah, I did, for quite a while I did that, yeah.
you left there to join And (inaudible) with Louis?

Yeah, I had my own group when I went with Louis. In fact, the little drummer that finally came with Louis from there, he was in my group, Danny Barcelona. He came over there. He was on my group over there.
How big a group?

Oh, we had -- I had about six pieces then at that time. I had a clarinet and trumpet and a -- myself, piano, drums, bass, about the same set up as Louis, that Louis had like that. And Louis used to come and sit in

with us almost -- after work almost every night when he was over there. Cozy Cole used to sit in with us. He was with Louis then. Barney Bigard, he would sit in with us. Yeah, because I was only working about four or five blocks away from where they were, and the guys I worked for were real swingers over there then.

I worked for two guys, and first thing they told me when I went there, they said, listen, don't pay any attention to us, because we've been married for 14 years together. They were two real swingers, man. One was from England, and one was from Phoenix, and they used to close the room at night when we got through, and they had people like Louis and them, and they would have champagne all over the place, champagne parties and send out and get all kind of food catered in to the place.

And you could go drink anything. I never saw a place like this before. They almost killed me, because I was drinking then. You could drink anything you wanted, and he -- in fact, he -- they gave me the run of the house. They told me -- told the bartender, anytime Trummy wants something, let him go pour his own. So I said, okay, man, and I was drinking every kind of thing you could name there.
I didn't remember how I got home sometimes, you know.
Which place was that?
This was Gibson's Bar. It was called the Circus Room upstairs in Honolulu, and Louis used to come up there and sit in with us all the time. Yeah.
How long did you work there?

I guess about a year, yeah, about a year, and that's where I left too. I would have stayed longer, but I left there to join Louis. I was up there when I came to join Louis. Oh, yeah, this place, wasn't a very big place, but it was jam packed all the time, you know. It was shorter hours, because at that time they didn't allow places to stay open late in Honolulu. We worked from about 8:00 to 12:00, something like that.
There was no dancing, just a small room, and I guess it seated about 80 comfortably, you know. And so it was called the Gibson Circus Room, just a bar.
Would -- all the clubs in Honolulu then were --

At that particular time, yeah. They -- but they had then what they -- any club with a liquor license had to close at 12:00 back there then when I went there, you know. But they changed later, but they had places that they used to get away with it, and they call them bottle clubs, and they were like private clubs. And you had like a key for your locker, and they used to stay open late. They used to open at 12:00, because I used to play that job, and then I'd

go out there and play one of those places from 12:00 to 4:00, and they used to rock, because, well, the guy couldn't sell drinks, but he could sell you a set up for maybe a dollar and a half or something, just a set up.
But, you know, you're not going to drink without having a, you know, chasers and ice and things of that sort. Actually, he's charging you for glasses is really what he's doing. And --
That's the way the after-hours joints in Los Angeles would work too.
(Inaudible)

Yeah, I guess all over they worked like that, more or less, you know, but it used to rock. These places used to, oh, used to go all night. And the bootleggers made a fortune around there because they'd keep liquor in their trunks of their cars, you know, and a guy want a bottle, he'd sneak him -- put it in his jacket and sneak it to a guy. Lot of service guys used to come out there and stay all night, you know.

Yeah, Honolulu was -- it used to swing back there then. But it's not like that now. They can open until 4:00 o'clock in the morning, but they -- you know, it's something funny. When a person figure they're sneaking and doing something, they'll do it more -- more of them will do it. Then when it becomes legal, not many of them want to do it, see.
(Laughter)
Strange, isn't it?
So you've been since you left Louis
in January '64?
'Inaudible' back in Hawaii (inaudible)?

Yeah, I went back in September. See, I left Louis in January because my wife was sick, and I went back, and that's when we found out what was wrong with her, when I got back, so she took treatments for a few months. And in the meantime I had to sell the house and get a lot of business straight.
So I left there in September. I left L. A. in September, going back, and I've been back since, only to come on visits or something like that, but I've never lived back on the mainland since then.
And for things like Dick Gibson's
And you come back (inaudible) -- and how often do you come back?

Oh, only about once a year. But since I've been on this particular job, I can only get away once a year. You know, I would have come back more often, but sometimes you got a steady job, you can't get away. I'm not getting rich on this job, but it -- in the meantime it's a living, you know. It keeps me playing.
Where do you work?
I work at Sheraton, the Waikiki Hotel, you know.
And you've been there how long?
Five years. I just signed a new one year contract. But I work up on the 30th floor, kind of over
the ocean, and it's glass enclosed, the room is. It's a nice room.
How big a group is it?

Just three guys and myself. Got a piano player, and he plays organ once in a while and piano and drums, and a guy plays the electric bass. I don't care too much for the electric bass, but I like the upright bass, you know, better, but --
Good, rich sound.
Yeah, I like it better. One of the reasons I got this guy, he sings fairly well, you know. When you got a little group, you got to utilize every little thing that you possibly can, you know.
Well, you do singing too, don't you?
Yeah, I do a lot of singing up there because --
As well as ----- but you had him singing, too, (inaudible).
-- there's dancing there. Well, we sing some four way things too, like some of the things I did with Lunceford, you know. We do some of those things.

But when you're playing for dancing, you got -- you have to usually do more singing because they want to hear lyrics, you know, a guy dancing with his chick out there, he wants to hear some lyrics and things. So you -- actually you do more singing than you would ordinarily when you -- if
you're playing for dancing, you know, unless you got a band like Basie's band that's really playing for swingers, you know.
We were talking about Big Miller (inaudible) the other day. I told you John Hendricks was looking for him. He worked in Hawaii for a while -- Honolulu didn't he? (inaudible).
Yeah, he was over there for a long while. In fact, when I went back over there, he was there. He wasn't there when I left, when I first left.
In the '60s-- what, '62, -3, he went a hit single over there and on his way back he went on a tour to Australia and had, I think (inaudible) stop in Honolulu, and he never came back, apparently.

Well, that's what happens to Big lot of times. I think he got stuck up in Canada somewhere now, you know. I don't know just where, but I can kind of get a kind of line on him from some musicians I know up there if I -- I'm going to write them and find out, let them know that John Hendricks is interested, and if I can find out that, where he is, I can write you back and let you know.
Sure. And John would like to use him on "Evolution of the Blues" in New York. from you (inaudible).
Well, he's good on that album, you know. I really liked him. I got the album, you know, and I really enjoy him, you know.
Was he singing? (inaudible) -- he wrote me once from Honolulu and said he was managing a club or something.
He was managing the club. I think he was singing too. He was managing and singing or something like that. Some -- couple of girls was running a club over there.
Betty Riley, (inaudible), huh?
Yeah. Yeah, he was singing and managing that club.
He was singing in Canada, so far as you know?
I heard he was. Somebody -- I forgot who told me, how long ago. It's been over a year since somebody -- or longer since -- but it's probably been since you've heard anything about it.
Yes. Yeah.

And it wasn't in a big city. It was somewhere up past Vancouver, farther up north there. It was some -- they told me the place. I forgot the place now, but I can find out from some of the musicians around Vancouver perhaps, you know. They would know.
today to Barry, Barry Martyn in the car, that you said you (inaudible). You your trombone til you're don't believe -- you can't really know (inaudible). You 60 years old.
Well --
You were 60 years old before (inaudible). you know your trombone.
-- I know a lot more about it now, because it's an intricate instrument. You see, it isn't like didn't make a trumpet where you put your finger down, the note is there, or

a saxophone, you put your fingers down, the note is there. There's no markings on that slide. You just got one piece of tubing to go by, and I'd put it this -- word it this way. I wish I knew half as much about that trombone. I was really blowing my brains out back there with Lunceford and them -- as I know now. I'll put it that way, you know.
There are so many things to learn about it, but at that time I was traveling too much to stop and concentrate on it. But it takes a long time to learn the trombone, to really learn it, you know.
What are the things you learned later?
It's kind of hard to explain. It's kind of hard to -- I couldn't just put my finger on it.
It's probably hard to put into words or feeling, the kind of --

Yeah, it's kind of rough to -- to really put it down in words, but there's so many things to learn about a trombone because, you know, weather affects that metal in the trombone a lot of times, and that's -- every slide is just a little bit different a fraction different on trombones, but these are things I didn't realize one time.
I probably had some good trombones and thought they were no good because I hadn't learned the horn yet. Things of that type, you know.
Do you have different slides?

No, I only use one. But I mean every slide, every time you get a horn with a slide, the tubing is just a fraction different, might be a farthing's different, a fraction different, but it might be enough to throw you off a little bit.
The reason I asked, it never occurred to me that someone would have more than one slide.
Oh, yeah, they have more than one slide.

But I know when I was in Berkeley in May Quentin Jackson flew out to do a recording date with Kenny Burrell and he was complaining the whole time he was there that in his rush for the plane he'd taken the wrong slide. He was very upset that he hadn't brought his favorite slide.
Well --
He brought one that he -- well, it was acceptable, but it wasn't his favorite.

Yeah, there are -- there are -- in fact, they build some cases to carry two slides, but I try to get two slides built the same way as possible if I had to, but I don't have two slides. I got two horns, and there's different slide on each horn. But I usually have my favorite horn. Now, just -- just gave me a horn, a new horn yesterday but I don't know it well enough to bother with it right now. I'd be afraid to just jump up and play it on the job until I really know it, but when I get back

I can experiment on it on a little dance job that I'm playing. You know, it wasn't -- if it doesn't work right, it won't hurt nothing, you know. But you certainly wouldn't go on a concert and bring a horn like that out for the first time.
(Reel Six.)
You were telling me about (inaudible) Some experiences that you had musically here in Los Angeles.

Yeah, this was way back when I was with Lunceford, and there was open way out by, out that way, called Honey's, and There wasn't nothing but open fields out there at that time. But T-Bone Walker used to go out there in fact, he was working out there, and I always liked the way he'd sing the blues. But you no longer (inaudible). So we used to go out there -Willie Smith, myself, Joe Thomas- after we got through work, but out there -- there would be a lot of musicians sittin' around, jamming. (inaudible) already out there, in those days. A guy (inaudible) played tenor sax And we'd go out there and back up (inaudible) out there all the time. (Inaudible) almost all night. He was (inaudible). But we'd go out there after work, and a lot of the people (inaudible). The only reason -- Art would work a club called Lovejoy (inaudible) out there because (inaudible).
I remember one night out there Ben Webster was up there (inaudible).
Uh-huh. What would this be, very early '30's, '41 or -- late '30's?
(Inaudible). I think it was more or less the '30's. (INaudible).
You remember what street it was on?
No, I don't know. (Inaudible).
No streets?
Not many. It was many then as it is now. And we used to go out there all night. We used to (inaudible) about 8:00, 9:00 in the morning. (Inaudible). And Cozy Cole was in that band (inaudible).
Where all did they work down here?

Well, they have the different ballrooms, and (inaudible), do one nighters and (inaudible) get together. There was a theater downtown called the Million Dollar Theater. There was (inaudible) on Central Avenue called the Plantation. (Inaudible) was up there. He had a little club around here somewhere.
Wasn't it an after hours club, yeah, the Black Flamingo, I think.
(Inaudible) a lot of different talents (inaudible).
Was there a lot happening on Central Avenue --
Well, (inaudible).
-- in the late '30's?
(Inaudible).
Then were there a lot of clubs during the late '30's. I know there were in the '40's, but were there in the late '30's?
(Inaudible) next to the Dunbar Hotel,
club down in there, and they (inaudible) down in there. I thought the Plantation was (inaudible). Wasn't it Apex and the (inaudible)?
I forget what it was, but there was a club there. I think it was the Plantation.
Yeah, it was further down there, I think.
Probably. I don't know. (Inaudible). There were a few spots around there, though. And there were quite a few good (inaudible) spots. I know (inaudible) early '40's and a guy named Eckles had a band.
Charlie Eckles, yeah, (inaudible) played with him on --
(Inaudible) and Eddie (inaudible) White.
Huh. I don't know about him.

(Inaudible) around back then, and (inaudible). I don't know where Marshall went to when he left Les Hite, but I know he used to work in Les H____'s band out in (inaudible). These were days when L. A. was something, and guys used to be after you, come out here and play for a while, you know, because (inaudible) -- there weren't too many places you (inaudible) three weeks, two, three weeks (inaudible).
And you go up north and play, and there wasn't a

lot of (inaudible) up there, and you play a lot of (inaudible) lot of ballrooms -- ballrooms all up around Oakland and (inaudible), and couple weeks playing just up around in there. (Inaudible) used to go out and play, come back, and we used to always play (inaudible).
And I left Hines, and about a month later I came back and there was (inaudible) Lunceford (inaudible).
(Laughter)
(Inaudible) playing like that, and I got a chance to jam a guy around town that I would never have (inaudible) a good band. I can't think of his last name. (Inaudible)
Yeah, well, he left Earl. I think he went to San Diego and put together a band at the place called the Club Royale for a long, long time.
(Inaudible).
I don't know whether the Club Royale is still there, but --
I don't know if (inaudible), but I know when we were in Honolulu we used to always (inaudible) out of Honolulu and go there (inaudible), and he was around there a long time. Oakland (inaudible).
San Francisco had some small clubs (inaudible)
(Inaudible segment)
You admired the doctor from Indiana. What was his name?
(Inaudible segment)
And tomorrow night you're going to be playing here in a tribute to Louis with Teddy Buckner, Barney Bigard, Dick Carey, Red Calendar and Cozy Cole.
(Inaudible).
When was the last time you played with Cozy?
(Inaudible) I don't know. Of course, about four years ago (inaudible) Honolulu, and I used to run a little dixieland place (inaudible).
(Inaudible segment)
