segments.title: Front matter
segments.summary: Copyright notice and title page for the Smithsonian interview of Trummy Young by Patricia Willard, Washington, Sept 17-18, 1976.

segments.title: Born in Savannah's Yamacraw section
segments.summary: Confirming his birth in Savannah in 1912 and his name, he describes the mixed neighborhood of Negroes, Indians and Italians where he grew up and the move to Lovers Lane.

segments.title: Savannah blues singers and the medicine shows
segments.summary: He recalls turpentine-field blues singers and the touring medicine shows with small bands, including clarinetist-comedian Wilton Crawley.

segments.title: The Jenkins Orphan Band marching through Savannah
segments.summary: Kids followed the Charleston orphanage band, which played jazz with dance steps; Jabbo Smith and trombonist John Nick played in it. Willard asks whether Cat Anderson was in it.

segments.title: Mixed neighborhood and schools in Savannah
segments.summary: Asked whether an integrated neighborhood was unusual, he says Indians, Negroes and Chinese went to the same schools, and Italians lived in their own section.

segments.title: Taking Frankie Rekuparo to the colored theater with charcoal on his face
segments.summary: A story of his Italian friend Frankie, whose father had a grocery, and the stunt of blackening Frankie's face to get into a Tom Mix movie at the Star Theater.

segments.title: First music he remembered: Bessie Smith records and guitar blues players
segments.summary: He remembers gramophone records of Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey and weekend guitar blues players from the turpentine fields.

segments.title: Blues as the language of the South; hearing "Margie"
segments.summary: Blues singers made up their own songs; few songs were written then; he first heard "Margie" at a fairground around 1920-21.

segments.title: Eagle-Eye Shields's band from Jacksonville
segments.summary: The small Jacksonville band that came through Savannah, and the later story of Edmund Hall and Cootie Williams's mother.

segments.title: Joe Oliver coming through Savannah
segments.summary: He saw Joe Oliver's band before Oliver went to Chicago; Louis was not with him then.

segments.title: Al Curren and the Snappy Six
segments.summary: A good local Savannah band, including a trombonist who later went to Europe whose name Young cannot recall.

segments.title: Musicians who came out of Savannah and Georgia
segments.summary: James Moody came from Savannah and Higginbotham from Atlanta; Young left Savannah in 1926 at 14.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: St. Emma's School in Virginia and its band
segments.summary: At 14 he went to a school near Richmond that had a band, where he began playing trombone.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Summers sitting in around Richmond; Bessie Smith at the Hippodrome
segments.summary: In summers he sat in with Johnson's Happy Pals and heard Bessie Smith at the Hippodrome Theater.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Bricklaying at school and leaving for Washington
segments.summary: He studied bricklaying at school, played on the side, and left for Washington where he began playing in bands.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Booker Coleman and Tommy Miles bands in Washington, with Jimmy Mundy
segments.summary: He lists his first big-band jobs, Booker Coleman's Hot Chocolates and Tommy Miles, with Elton Hill and Jimmy Mundy, and Eckstine and Tyree Glenn later in the Miles band.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Battles of music with the Ambassadors from Baltimore
segments.summary: The Miles band played battles with the Baltimore Ambassadors, with a high-note trumpeter Stevenson who later joined Lunceford and the Horton brothers.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Tommy Miles band personnel
segments.summary: He names the pianist Garnett Clark, the size of the band and its saxophones, trombones, trumpets and rhythm section.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Billy Eckstine and Bill Kenney at Howard Theater amateur night
segments.summary: Eckstine joined as a singer after competing weekly with Bill Kenney in amateur contests at the Howard Theater.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Manager Bailey's fifty cents, Tommy Miles's beans, and the Howard pit band
segments.summary: The manager Bailey paid the band fifty cents each; Miles fed them at home; they played the Club Prudome and the Howard Theater pit.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: The Hardy Brothers show band and the theater circuit
segments.summary: He worked in the Hardy Brothers band, led by Coleridge Davis, his first show band, and describes the Lafayette and Alhambra circuit and the tree of hope.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Summer in Asbury Park with Booker Coleman
segments.summary: The Hot Chocolates played a summer for Reece Dupree in Asbury Park, paid in potatoes and small money, with extra pay on Father Divine nights.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Playing for Father Divine's meetings
segments.summary: He describes opening Father Divine's meetings with hot songs and hymns while hired preachers did the preaching.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Booker Coleman's band personnel
segments.summary: He names the members of the Hot Chocolates, including guitarist-violinist Jimmy Holmes, and the size of the band.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Bellhops and Hot Chocolates uniforms; dances and fairs
segments.summary: Coleman first called the band the Bellhops, then Hot Chocolates; they played fairs and dances around Norfolk and Richmond.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: The "Chocolate Stomp," Mundy and Goodman, and head arrangements
segments.summary: He says "Swingtime in the Rockies" began as the band's "Chocolate Stomp," and compares such head arrangements to Basie's early book.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Arrangers in the Tommy Miles band
segments.summary: Most of Miles's book was written, by arrangers like Jimmy Mundy, Elton Hill and Garnett Clark.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Writing "A Lover Is Blue" and "Traveling Light"
segments.summary: He started composing; Mundy arranged "Traveling Light" and claimed the tune, and Johnny Mercer wrote lyrics.

segments.chapter: Virginia school and first Washington bands
segments.title: Missing royalties and his friendship with Mundy
segments.summary: His name was added later, after missing the first royalties; he says Billie Holiday's book reports $75 each, and he held no grudge against his friend.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Fooling around with instruments in Savannah
segments.summary: He hung around local musicians, played with Georgia Red's trombone, and thought the old blues players were the best.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Trumpet, drums, then trombone; self-taught
segments.summary: He tried trumpet and drums before the trombone, which he first played seriously at school in 1926 and took lessons on later.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Influences: the Jenkins band trombonists and Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: His uncle did not influence him; the Jenkins Orphan Band did, and then Louis Armstrong; the Jenkins boys were about 13 to 18.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: His family and Savannah migrants to New York
segments.summary: He has sisters and half brothers, an uncle Will who played trombone, and says Savannah people went to New York as New Orleans people went to Chicago.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: How he got the name Trummy
segments.summary: His parents called him James O.; Booker Coleman, who could not remember names, called him Trummy; he corrects Chilton and discusses mislabeled Lunceford records.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Always wanting to be a musician; the military school
segments.summary: He wanted to be a professional all his life and the drilling at the military school confirmed it.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Band instruction at school under John Scott
segments.summary: They played marches and overtures, jazzed things up, and were taught by John Scott, a clarinetist.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Studying with Jaroslav Cimera in Chicago
segments.summary: After joining Hines he took lessons from the Polish teacher, prompted by Billy Franklin and Louis Taylor, and became his most apt student.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: How trombonists played then and hearing Arthur Pryor
segments.summary: Trombonists then only slid; hearing bandmaster Arthur Pryor's command made him want to play differently.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Experimenting with Earl Hines and the Down Beat criticism
segments.summary: He tried high and daring things at the Grand Terrace, and a Down Beat review calling him atrocious sent him practicing eight hours a day.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Hearing Pryor in concert; buying his first trombone
segments.summary: He heard Pryor at band concerts in Richmond and Washington and bought his first trombone in a Washington pawn shop.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Learning to care for a slide; no help from older trombonists
segments.summary: A machinist at the Olds factory taught him slide care; Jimmy Harrison and others would not help, so he helps kids today.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Jam sessions as the training ground
segments.summary: Constant after-hours playing taught them, in basements and anywhere, and new arrivals were challenged.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Eddie Durham finds Charlie Christian in Oklahoma City
segments.summary: With Lunceford, the band heard a guitarist in a club; Eddie Durham went to cut him and found Charlie Christian.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: After-hours jam spots in New York
segments.summary: Basement and speakeasy spots by instrument night, Mexico's, the 101 Ranch, the Elks and the Rhythm Club.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Jamming at the DeLisa in Chicago
segments.summary: He jammed nightly at Mike DeLisa's with Albert Ammons and others while Roy Eldridge and Chu Berry were with Fletcher; the union later curtailed it.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Minton's, Monroe's and carrying your own rhythm section
segments.summary: Minton's and Monroe's held sessions, and horn players brought their own rhythm sections, but real jams meant playing with strangers.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Faddis and Eubie Blake at Dick Gibson's Colorado party
segments.summary: At Gibson's jazz party in Colorado, 22-year-old Faddis played with 94-year-old Eubie Blake, filmed for a movie.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Why playing with unfamiliar musicians matters
segments.summary: Playing with new people changes your ideas; he enjoys playing swing alongside modern trombonists.

segments.chapter: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
segments.title: Lineup of the Dick Gibson jazz party
segments.summary: He lists the trombones, trumpets, saxophones and rhythm players and reads out how Gibson boxes the sets.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Leaving Tommy Miles for Earl Hines; Tyree Glenn and Eckstine
segments.summary: Mundy went to Hines first and brought Young; Tyree Glenn replaced him in Miles's band, and Eckstine sang regularly only after.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Earl Hines's singers and a loose band vs Lunceford's discipline
segments.summary: Hines had singers Herb Jeffries and Arthur Lee Simkins, and Young did not want to leave a free band for strict Lunceford.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Ray Nance persuades him to join Lunceford
segments.summary: Ray Nance urged him to go, saying he would get a better shot, and saw him off at the train.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Earl Hines's bus accident tour and the Mills Brothers show
segments.summary: On a theater tour from Des Moines to Minneapolis in late 1933, tenor Cecil Irwin was killed; the show included the Mills Brothers, Palmer Brothers and Tip Tap and Toe.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: The Palmer Brothers and Grand Terrace shows
segments.summary: He remembers the Palmer Brothers, his early record "Rhythm Lullaby" with Hines, and Andy Razaf's Grand Terrace shows where Tip Tap and Toe first danced on a drum.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: The bus accident in Iowa
segments.summary: A grain truck sideswiped the band bus; Cecil Irwin was killed, and Young broke his ankle.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Hearing Lester Young at the Cotton Club in Minneapolis
segments.summary: They urged Hines to hire a tenor player in a Minneapolis club, Lester Young in tennis shoes, but Hines chose Budd Johnson because Lester reportedly did not read.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Touring in summers and jamming around Chicago
segments.summary: The Grand Terrace closed in summers, so Young toured or played around Chicago with Albert Ammons, Guy Kelly and Israel Crosby.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Gigs around Chicago with Tiny Parham, Roy Eldridge and others
segments.summary: He took casual jobs with Tiny Parham, Roy Eldridge, Punch Miller, Minor Hall, Carroll Dickerson and Horace Henderson.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: John Collins's mother's band, Joe Williams and Bird at DeLisa's
segments.summary: A barbershop group with Dan Grissom singing, Joe Williams as doorman at the Regal, and Charlie Parker sitting in at DeLisa's.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Choosing Earl Hines over Chick Webb
segments.summary: He had only played New York theaters in shows, and chose Hines over Webb because he liked Jimmy Mundy's arrangements.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Sandy Williams, and turning down Cab Calloway and Fletcher
segments.summary: He stayed with Hines for the friends and the chance to solo on broadcasts, and refused Calloway, who he felt did not let his men feature.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Pay and show rehearsals at the Grand Terrace
segments.summary: He earned about $44 a week, at most $68, playing three long shows nightly; shows were rehearsed for weeks.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Arrangers for Hines and for Lunceford
segments.summary: Mundy, Cecil Irwin and others wrote for Hines, and Lunceford's band had many unsung arrangers such as Billy Moore, Eddie Durham and Don Redman.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Martha Raye singing at the Grand Terrace; Joe E. Lewis
segments.summary: A young Martha Raye sang with the band after her Loop job; Sally Rand and Joe E. Lewis were around in 1933.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: The colored hotel above the Grand Terrace
segments.summary: Visiting black bands stayed at the hotel next to the Grand Terrace, and musicians jammed in the rooms.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Jamming with Ellington men and Fats Waller at the hotel
segments.summary: He recalls Lawrence Brown, Cootie Williams, Johnny Hodges, Arthur Whetsel and Harry Carney, and Fats Waller with a rented organ.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Chicago theaters and Earl Hines going out to play
segments.summary: The Oriental Theater show with Milton Berle, and Hines taking men out to play all night.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Art Tatum in Chicago and Los Angeles
segments.summary: Tatum cut down every piano player, and Young later lived in the same Los Angeles apartment building as Tatum.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: The Los Angeles apartment building and Joe Louis
segments.summary: They work out the address of the building owned by Della Miles, where Willie Best and others lived; Joe Louis lived nearby.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Working with Roy Eldridge at Billy Berg's
segments.summary: After a JATP tour, Young worked a few weeks at Berg's with Roy Eldridge, Anita O'Day, Willie Smith and Wardell Gray.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Jamming with Roy Eldridge and Ammons versus working with them
segments.summary: He jammed but never worked with them in Chicago, and distinguishes a one-night pickup from working with a leader.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Raymond Scott's band and Young's own bands on 52nd Street
segments.summary: He played in Scott's studio band and led a band at the Yacht Club with John Malachi and Tommy Potter, another with Dexter Gordon, after Chicago's Capital Lounge.

segments.chapter: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
segments.title: Backing Billie Holiday with Tiny Grimes, with Art Tatum on the bill
segments.summary: He played about six months in Tiny Grimes's band at the Yacht Club, backing Holiday, with Tatum the other act.

segments.title: Joining Jimmie Lunceford with Ted Buckner
segments.summary: He went to New York to join Lunceford with alto man Ted Buckner, who played the first chorus on "Margie".

segments.title: Singing "Margie" and Sy Oliver writing the background
segments.summary: After September 1937 rehearsals, Young sang "Margie" on the train and Sy Oliver wrote the arrangement around his vocal in D.

segments.title: Writing "'Tain't What You Do" with Sy Oliver
segments.summary: He hummed a tune from a Chicago drinking spot and wrote the song with Sy Oliver one Sunday in Nashville.

segments.title: Other compositions and writing with Lunceford
segments.summary: He describes "Easy Does It," a song for Billie Holiday, "Traveling Light" as his best melody, and Lunceford's encouragement.

segments.title: Recording "Margie" and recording bands
segments.summary: They rehearsed "Margie" in a theater dressing room and recorded it for Decca before playing it on a job; Andy Kirk was another good recording band.

segments.title: Lunceford's ninety one-nighters and being refused food
segments.summary: The band played endless one-nighters, and Will Smith, who looks white, bought sandwiches for the band where they were not served.

segments.title: Willie Smith and Harry James's mixed band
segments.summary: Willard tells how Willie Smith, who looks white, passed in Harry James's band and was a convenience when food was hard to get.

segments.title: Hotel refused in Providence with Benny Goodman; Charlie Barnett and Boyd Raeburn
segments.summary: Young, Teddy Wilson and Slam Stewart were refused a hotel room; Goodman did not fight it, unlike Barnett and Raeburn.

segments.title: Boyd Raeburn's tours and who enforced segregation
segments.summary: Raeburn's band toured New England, Jersey and Virginia; often the proprietor, not the law, objected to a mixed band.

segments.title: Earl Hines's Southern dates and meeting Texas and Arkansas players
segments.summary: Hines's all-black band played the South, where Young met Illinois Jacquet, Cleanhead and Milt Larkin's band in Houston and Al Hibbler in Little Rock.

segments.title: Chartered buses from Newark
segments.summary: Bands chartered buses that broke down often; he says love of music made up for the hardship.

segments.title: Rooming houses and home cooking in the South
segments.summary: Bands stayed in private homes or rooming houses, ate home-cooked meals and knew hosts in many towns.

segments.title: Willie Smith's superstitions
segments.summary: Young says Smith was superstitious in the Lunceford band and grew more so with James and Ellington.

segments.title: Duke Ellington wrote for his players and loved his band
segments.summary: Ellington wrote for players once he knew their strengths, called the band his toy, and kept touring after paying his dues.

segments.title: Harry Carney driving for Duke
segments.summary: Carney was quiet and liked to drive, a good match for Ellington, who did not want conversation.

segments.title: Duke visiting Honolulu; music as his life
segments.summary: Ellington visited Young in Honolulu before his death, marveled that Young used a plunger, and was always composing; Willard describes his portable piano.

segments.title: Duke's favorite tune and re-arranging "Come Sunday"
segments.summary: Ellington grew tired of a finished tune and kept rearranging it, as "Come Sunday" featured Hodges, then Ray Nance and Bunny Briggs.

segments.title: Why he never worked with Duke
segments.summary: Contracts with Raymond Scott and a 52nd Street club kept him from joining Ellington, and club owners paid by name value.

segments.title: Norman Granz's JATP tours
segments.summary: Young did about three Jazz at the Philharmonic tours, only in the US and Canada.

segments.title: Martha Glaser, Granz's secretary
segments.summary: Glaser started as Granz's secretary, scaled theaters sharply, and later managed Erroll Garner.

segments.title: Granz's first jam sessions in Los Angeles
segments.summary: Granz ran small sessions in L.A. paying $9; Young, Willie Smith, Nat Cole and Red Callender played, and Granz later paid well and traveled first class.

segments.title: Granz insisting on unsegregated audiences
segments.summary: Young saw Granz refuse to play in Lexington and Norfolk unless seating was mixed, and says money talks.

segments.title: Prejudice, education and kids playing together
segments.summary: He agrees with Ellington that prejudice is economic, says everyone has prejudices, and notes children of all nationalities play together in Honolulu.

segments.title: Burying his mother in Savannah and the policeman at the wake
segments.summary: At his mother's wake white musician friends came, and a polite policeman asked them to leave.

segments.title: Progress in Georgia and music breaking barriers
segments.summary: He and Willard discuss changes in Georgia, music breaking barriers, and friends on both sides in the South.

segments.title: His first recording and discographies
segments.summary: His first recording was with Earl Hines in Chicago around 1933; he hopes Stanley Dance can help with his book.

segments.title: Why he loves Dick Gibson's jazz party
segments.summary: He praises the party's closeness and organization, with Gibson improvising set combinations such as Faddis and Eubie Blake.

segments.title: Earl Hines band personnel: Walter Fuller and the "Rosetta" re-creation
segments.summary: Day two begins with Walter Fuller, who sang "Rosetta," a late-1960s recreation of the record, and other Hines men like Quinn Wilson.

segments.title: Ray Nance in Earl Hines's band
segments.summary: Nance was his closest friend in the band, a violinist and Louis-style trumpeter and showman, whom Ellington praised.

segments.title: Getting solos with Lunceford; Hines let players grow
segments.summary: Joining Lunceford made his name, since there was no featured trombonist; Hines had given him room to develop.

segments.title: His first Lunceford recordings; Herb Flemming remembered
segments.summary: He is unsure which record was first, recalls "Margie" and "Annie Laurie," and remembers the Savannah trombonist as Herb Flemming.

segments.title: The Lunceford vocal trio becomes a quartet
segments.summary: Sy Oliver, Eddie Tompkins and Willie Smith had recorded "My Blue Heaven"; Young joined to make a quartet that did "Ain't She Sweet" and "Cheatin' on Me," while Dan Grissom sang ballads.

segments.title: Second transcript section: Tapes 4-6
segments.summary: Title page for tapes 4 to 6, September 18 and 20, 1976, with the start of the proceedings.

segments.title: Dan Grissom and the entertaining Lunceford band
segments.summary: Grissom sang ballads while the others did rhythm tunes; Joe Thomas also sang, and the band was good to watch.

segments.title: The Dandridge Sisters on Lunceford theater tours
segments.summary: The trio, with Etta Jones who later married Gerald Wilson, looked good and toured theaters with the band.

segments.title: Backing Bill Robinson and other acts
segments.summary: Lunceford's band spent 22 weeks of theaters backing Bojangles Robinson, and also backed chorus lines and acts like Buck and Bubbles.

segments.title: Theater schedules: four shows a day, week-long runs
segments.summary: Theaters ran about four shows a day, five on weekends, plus an Apollo midnight show, with one-week engagements.

segments.title: Eating near the theaters and the Braddock Bar
segments.summary: Cooks like Mom Baker fed musicians for 50 cents, performers gathered at the Braddock Bar, and the four-city circuit was called around the world.

segments.title: Charlie Barnet's band personnel
segments.summary: He recalls Bunny Briggs dancing with Barnet, and members including Al Killian, Chubby Jackson, Ralph Burns, Buddy DeFranco and singer Virginia Maxey.

segments.title: Leaving Lunceford over too many one-nighters; manager Harold Oxley
segments.summary: He left because of the one-nighters, said manager Oxley booked many, and notes the band's hits and many college dates.

segments.title: Jimmie Lunceford as a person
segments.summary: Lunceford was quiet, did not drink or curse, was strict about uniforms and punctuality with fines, and was like a school teacher.

segments.title: Lunceford's Fisk origins and hits before Young joined
segments.summary: The founding members came from Fisk; Lunceford was already successful when Young joined.

segments.title: Lunceford's labels and New York as the recording center
segments.summary: Most recordings were made in New York for Decca and Columbia; the industry later moved to Los Angeles.

segments.title: Duke Ellington in a class by himself
segments.summary: Ellington had hits from his own compositions before any of the others.

segments.title: Hearing Duke at the Lincoln Colonnade in Washington
segments.summary: He heard Ellington's band at dances at the Lincoln Colonnade and got to know the young Ellington men.

segments.title: Big bands passing through Washington
segments.summary: Fletcher Henderson, Chick Webb, Zack White, Jess Williams and Small's Paradise bands all came to Washington.

segments.title: Trombonists in Fletcher Henderson's band
segments.summary: He heard Higginbotham, Sandy Williams, Claude Jones in a wig, Rex Stewart and Jimmy Harrison.

segments.title: First seeing Louis Armstrong at the Howard Theater
segments.summary: He saw Armstrong in Washington about 1930, once giving him a knife for a corn; Armstrong later said he overblew then.

segments.title: What he learned from Louis about preserving himself
segments.summary: Watching Armstrong, Young learned to rest, not eat a big meal before playing, and not play too many high choruses at rehearsal.

segments.title: Louis's musical directors and rehearsing for TV
segments.summary: Armstrong rarely rehearsed bands himself; Billy Kyle and earlier Joe Garland and Louis Russell handled it.

segments.title: Movies with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: He did "The Glenn Miller Story," "High Society," "The Five Pennies" and European films with Armstrong.

segments.title: "Blues in the Night" with Lunceford at the Casa Manana
segments.summary: His first film was Warner Brothers' "Blues in the Night" filmed while the band played the Casa Manana in Culver City.

segments.title: Edward R. Murrow's European short with Armstrong
segments.summary: A 90-minute film on a European tour, narrated by Murrow, with a flight over the Alps and playing with Bechet in Paris.

segments.title: Salaries in Lunceford's band
segments.summary: Young earned $10 a night on one-nighters, Willie Smith more, and Sy Oliver was paid $5 for arranging and copying "Blue Heaven."

segments.title: $33 for the "Margie" record date
segments.summary: A three-hour record date paid scale of $33, with no royalties though "Margie" sold in the millions.

segments.title: New Era Publishing and royalties
segments.summary: His tunes went into Lunceford and Oxley's publishing house, and he took it to an arbitration board for a little money.

segments.title: Why the band broke up: pay, road and buses
segments.summary: Pay and the hard road led men to leave; the band held a meeting at the Harlem YMCA about leaking buses.

segments.title: Leaking buses, bad jumps and driving accidents
segments.summary: He rested a month before Barnet; he describes long jumps, Russell Bowles's accident, and Chu Berry's death.

segments.title: Bands traveling in cars
segments.summary: Some bands, perhaps Andy Kirk's, traveled in cars with one instrument truck.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: His apartment at 555 Edgecombe
segments.summary: He lived at 555 Edgecombe, with Don Redman next door and Joe Louis and Erskine Hawkins in the building, and later gave the apartment to Johnny Hodges.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Joining Charlie Barnet at the Park Central Hotel
segments.summary: Barnet worked briefly, loved Duke and patterned his band on Ellington, with arrangements by Andy Gibson.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Barnet paid better than Lunceford
segments.summary: Barnet had family money and paid Young about $50 a week more; he stayed about a year and did not record with him.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Playing around New York; Boyd Raeburn; leading his own band
segments.summary: After Barnet he played small jobs, a few months with Raeburn, and formed his own band from November 1943.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: His own small bands on 52nd Street and in Chicago
segments.summary: His band had Dexter Gordon, Curly Russell, Denzil Best and Jimmy Jones, and a later group of Washington players at Chicago's Capitol Lounge.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: 52nd Street clubs and rooms
segments.summary: Every room had a name act, Erroll Garner, Dizzy Gillespie's group and Eddie Heywood among them.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: John Kirby's band at the Onyx and the White Rose Bar
segments.summary: Kirby's sextet rehearsed six months before its first job, and musicians drank at the White Rose Bar around the corner.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Jimmy Ryan's, Leo Watson and Basie at the Famous Door
segments.summary: Bechet played at Jimmy Ryan's with Vic Dickenson and Leo Watson, and Basie's 14-piece band crammed into the tiny Famous Door.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Kelly's Stables: everyone in a tiny room, nobody paid
segments.summary: Hawkins, Billy Daniels and Nat Cole all played Kelly's Stables for about $100 a week; Kirby's band eventually earned a little.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: New York as the center of everything; small-group record dates
segments.summary: Everything happened in New York, and he first recorded with small groups with Dizzy, Parker and Don Byas.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Timme Rosenkrantz's apartment recordings of Erroll Garner
segments.summary: A collector recorded Garner by the hour and later issued the records cheaply in Europe, undercutting Garner's sales.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Bootleg recorders at Armstrong concerts in Europe
segments.summary: In Europe from 1952 with Louis, pirates hid recording equipment in concert halls that the road manager could not find.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Recording with Dizzy, Parker and Don Byas; Clyde Hart
segments.summary: Young recorded with Dizzy and Parker without working steadily with them, including "Can't Get Started," and with pianist-arranger Clyde Hart.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Rubberlegs Williams and Johnny Hodges; the Bessie Smith songs date
segments.summary: Willard asks about the Continental date; Young describes Rubberlegs Williams's behavior and the Bessie Smith songs recorded.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: The benzedrine coffee record date
segments.summary: Parker soaked a benzedrine inhaler in coffee, Rubberlegs drank it by mistake and went wild during the session.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Tunes and arrangements on the Rubberlegs date
segments.summary: Young sang four vocals; Clyde Hart arranged, and Hart died of TB not long after.

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: Tadd Dameron's "Good Beat" and the Cozy Cole date
segments.summary: He made "Good Beat" with Dizzy and led-by-Cozy date with Hawkins, Earl Hines, Joe Thomas and Billy Taylor, including his tune "Through for the Night."

segments.chapter: Barnet, 52nd Street and New York recording dates
segments.title: More New York record dates: Sarah Vaughan, Buck Clayton, Eckstine
segments.summary: He recorded with Tony Scott and Sarah Vaughan, with Buck Clayton for John Hammond, and in Eckstine's big band.

segments.title: Invited to Hawaii with C. P. Johnson's band
segments.summary: After a Granz tour and Berg's, he joined Gerald Wilson's friends in C. P. Johnson's band for six weeks in Hawaii with Red Callender and Dexter Gordon.

segments.title: Unpaid in Hawaii; staying and marrying
segments.summary: The leader C. P. Johnson had taken the band's pay in advance because of a narcotics charge; Young stayed in Hawaii and married there.

segments.title: Leaving Louis Armstrong because his wife was ill
segments.summary: After 12 years with Armstrong, he left in 1964 to care for his wife, who had cancer, and Joe Glaser was angry.

segments.title: Louis's understanding and generosity
segments.summary: Armstrong later understood in Honolulu, and Young says he was warm and generous without wanting publicity.

segments.title: Louis keeping him up to coach Tyree Glenn; learning from Armstrong
segments.summary: Armstrong kept Young up all night in Honolulu to teach Tyree Glenn the vocal spots; Young learned timing and phrasing from him.

segments.title: The Goodman-Armstrong tour and showmanship
segments.summary: Benny Goodman put Armstrong on first, then last on John Hammond's advice, and complained of clowning; Young says Louis was both musician and showman.

segments.title: Louis and Duke were unteachable originals
segments.summary: Nobody taught Louis or Duke their ways; Billie Holiday, Sinatra and Crosby all listened to Armstrong.

segments.title: What Young learned: timing, building a solo, stage presentation
segments.summary: From Armstrong he learned to build slowly, relax on stage and read an audience.

segments.title: John Hendricks and the Armstrong-Ellington record
segments.summary: Hendricks also watched Louis closely; Young enjoyed the record of Armstrong's band with Duke at the piano.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet
segments.summary: Willard cites Duke's four favorites; Young calls Bechet daring and reckless, jammed with him in Paris, and notes the statue in France.

segments.title: Traveling first class with Louis; his bad heart
segments.summary: Armstrong's tours were hard but first class; he had heart trouble and a heart attack at Spoleto.

segments.title: Armstrong's congestion and daily laxative
segments.summary: Armstrong coughed constantly, slept in a fan's draft, and took Pluto Water then Swiss Kriss every night, per his doctor.

segments.title: Louis's and Duke's itineraries and Glaser's favoritism
segments.summary: Willard compares Armstrong's lighter itineraries with Ellington's; Duke complained Glaser gave Louis better dates.

segments.title: How Joe Glaser became Louis's manager
segments.summary: Louis fired his manager Collins after John Hammond knocked Collins down for a slur, and asked Glaser to take over.

segments.title: Glaser's handshake deal and handling Louis's money
segments.summary: They never had a contract, and Glaser kept Louis's money safe, leaving him and Lucille millions.

segments.title: Glaser and Louis depended on each other; Glaser managing Duke
segments.summary: Glaser cared about Louis and died shortly before him; Young was glad Glaser's office also got Duke lucrative work.

segments.title: Louis as adviser to statesmen; staying with Tshombe
segments.summary: Young marvels that world leaders consulted Armstrong, who scolded Tshombe, and the band feared for his safety at Tshombe's house.

segments.title: Louis's replies to the press in Beirut and Cairo
segments.summary: Asked why he would play for Israel, Louis said a note is a note in any language; in Cairo he told reporters he had a trumpet and a young wife.

segments.title: Ernie Anderson, the Pope, and Doc Pugh
segments.summary: Publicist Ernie Anderson tells how Louis answered the Pope's question about children, and Louis's quip about his valet Doc Pugh's death.

segments.title: Louis's constant humor
segments.summary: Young says Armstrong's quips came off the top of his head and kept him in stitches.

segments.title: Louis on modern paintings at the Louvre
segments.summary: Armstrong told Young the Russians put the modern paintings up to confuse Americans.

segments.title: Princess Margaret, Prince Akihito, the "black Buddha" and the catcher's mitt
segments.summary: Stories of Armstrong holding court with royalty, dancing with the Japanese princess, and wearing a catcher's mitt to protect his lip.

segments.title: Paul Baron's orchestra on the Mildred Bailey radio show
segments.summary: He was a regular on Mildred Bailey's show with Teddy Wilson and Charlie Shavers, and played in Raymond Scott's band, for about a season.

segments.title: Two months with Claude Hopkins at the Hurricane Club
segments.summary: He played about two months with Hopkins, with Joe Garland and Rudy Powell in the band.

segments.title: Norman Granz tours in 1946 and 1947
segments.summary: He made two tours of eight to ten weeks, not two years; Granz kept only Ella and Oscar Peterson steadily.

segments.title: Boyd Raeburn's band with Dizzy, Chaloff and Bothwell
segments.summary: He recalls the Raeburn band's personnel, including George Handy's writing, and does not remember recording with it.

segments.title: A few months with Benny Goodman
segments.summary: In 1945 he played one-nighters and a week at Steel Pier with Goodman, with Slam Stewart and Red Norvo.

segments.title: Tiny Grimes engagements
segments.summary: He worked with Grimes twice, once backing Billie Holiday.

segments.title: First clubs in Honolulu and the Brown Derby trio
segments.summary: After C. P. Johnson's band he played the Hula Rhumba and island concerts, and the Brown Derby with a trio whose bassist Art played badly.

segments.title: His Honolulu group at the Circus Room, with Louis sitting in
segments.summary: He led a sextet that included drummer Danny Barcelona at the Gibson Circus Room, where Louis, Cozy Cole and Barney Bigard sat in nightly.

segments.title: Honolulu bottle clubs and closing hours
segments.summary: Clubs closed at midnight, but bottle clubs stayed open to 4 a.m. selling set-ups, and bootleggers prospered.

segments.title: Returning to Hawaii in September 1964
segments.summary: After his wife's treatments he sold the house in Los Angeles and moved back to Honolulu, visiting the mainland only occasionally.

segments.title: Playing the Sheraton Waikiki and singing for dancers
segments.summary: He has worked five years at the Sheraton Waikiki in a quartet, singing more because dancers want lyrics.

segments.title: Big Miller in Honolulu and Canada
segments.summary: They discuss singer Big Miller, who stayed in Hawaii and may now be in Canada, for John Hendricks's project.

segments.title: Still learning the trombone after sixty
segments.summary: He says he knows far more about the instrument now, since a slide has no markings.

segments.title: Slides and horns: favorite instrument
segments.summary: Willard mentions Quentin Jackson's slide; Young has two horns with different slides and tries new horns on small jobs first.

segments.title: After-hours jamming in Los Angeles and T-Bone Walker
segments.summary: On Lunceford trips he, Willie Smith and Joe Thomas jammed at a club out in the fields, where T-Bone Walker worked and Ben Webster showed up (mostly inaudible).

segments.title: Central Avenue and other West Coast spots
segments.summary: Willard and Young recall the Million Dollar Theater, the Plantation, the Dunbar Hotel and ballrooms around Oakland and San Francisco (much is inaudible).

segments.title: Closing: the Louis tribute concert
segments.summary: Inaudible passages and Willard's note about the next night's tribute to Louis with Teddy Buckner, Barney Bigard and Cozy Cole.
